title: EC2 to S3 Access: IAM Role vs Access Keys
description: A developer is building an application that runs on an EC2 instance and needs to write objects to an S3 bucket. A colleague suggests embedding AWS access keys directly in the application's configuration file. You need to advise on the best practice approach for granting this EC2 instance permission to write to S3.
hints: Think about what happens if the EC2 instance is compromised or the config file is accidentally committed to Git.
AWS has a built-in mechanism specifically designed to grant AWS services permissions to other AWS services.
Consider which approach eliminates the need to manage, rotate, or store long-term credentials entirely.

solution.explanation: IAM Roles attached to EC2 instances (via Instance Profiles) are the AWS best practice because they provide temporary, automatically rotated credentials through the Instance Metadata Service — eliminating the need to store, manage, or rotate long-term access keys. When an IAM Role is assigned to an EC2 instance, the AWS SDK automatically discovers and uses these credentials through the credential provider chain without any code changes. Embedding access keys in configuration files is dangerous because long-term credentials can be accidentally committed to source control, exposed in logs or AMI snapshots, or stolen if the instance is compromised — and they remain valid until manually revoked. The IAM Role approach follows the principle of least privilege because you grant only the specific S3 actions needed (e.g., s3:PutObject on a specific bucket) rather than broad permissions. On the exam, any scenario asking how an AWS service should access another AWS service will almost always have 'IAM Role' as the correct answer — access keys stored anywhere are almost always wrong. A common exam trap is an answer that says 'create an IAM User for the application' — this is inferior to roles because it still uses long-term credentials.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Instance Profile vs IAM Role
methodSignatures.description: An Instance Profile is the container that holds an IAM Role for EC2 — when the console says 'attach IAM role to EC2', it's actually creating/using an Instance Profile. In the CLI/CFN you must create them separately. The exam uses both terms.

The AWS SDK checks credentials in this order: (1) Environment variables, (2) Java system properties, (3) AWS credentials profile file, (4) ECS container credentials, (5) EC2 Instance Metadata. On EC2, step 5 (IMDS) is where instance role credentials come from.

A trust policy (Principal) on the role must explicitly allow the EC2 service (ec2.amazonaws.com) to assume the role via sts:AssumeRole. Without this trust relationship, EC2 cannot use the role even if the permission policies are correct.

title: Managing 50 Developer Permissions Efficiently with IAM Groups
description: A company has 50 developers who all need read access to a specific set of S3 buckets and the ability to invoke Lambda functions. New developers are onboarded frequently and some move between teams. The security team wants a scalable, maintainable way to manage these permissions without assigning policies to each user individually.
hints: IAM has a concept that allows you to group users together and assign permissions to the group rather than each individual.
Think about what happens when you need to add a new permission for all 50 developers — how many policy updates do you need with the optimal approach?
Consider also how you would handle a developer moving from the 'backend' team to the 'frontend' team.

solution.explanation: IAM Groups provide a scalable mechanism for managing permissions across multiple users by allowing you to attach policies once at the group level rather than managing them per-user. This dramatically reduces operational overhead: adding a new permission requires a single group policy update instead of 50 individual updates. When a new developer joins, you simply add them to the relevant group and they immediately inherit all required permissions. When someone leaves or changes roles, group membership changes handle the permission update cleanly. A critical exam point is that IAM Groups are NOT principals — you cannot reference a group in the Principal field of a resource-based policy (like an S3 bucket policy); you can only reference IAM Users, Roles, and AWS services there. Another common exam trap is that groups cannot be nested — you cannot put a group inside another group. The most efficient architecture combines IAM Groups (for user management) with IAM Roles (for service-to-service access).

methodSignatures.description: IAM Groups cannot be used as a Principal in trust policies or resource-based policies (S3 bucket policies, KMS key policies, etc.). Only IAM Users, IAM Roles, AWS accounts, and AWS services can be Principals. This is a frequent exam trap.
IAM Groups cannot contain other groups — only IAM Users. There is no hierarchy. If you need hierarchical permissions, use IAM Roles with permission boundaries or AWS Organizations with SCPs instead.

title: IAM Policy vs Permission Boundary vs SCP: Understanding the Difference
description: A senior developer needs to explain the three key layers of IAM permission control to their team: IAM Identity Policies, Permission Boundaries, and Service Control Policies (SCPs). Each layer serves a different purpose and applies in a different context. Understanding when each applies is critical for architecting secure, multi-account AWS environments.
hints: Think about the difference between granting permissions and setting maximum permission limits.
SCPs apply at the AWS Organization/Account level — they constrain entire accounts, not just individual users.
An effective permission is the INTERSECTION of what all applicable policies allow — the most restrictive combination wins.

solution.explanation: IAM Identity Policies are what most developers think of as 'permissions' — they explicitly grant (or deny) access to AWS resources for specific users or roles. Permission Boundaries work as a safety net when you delegate permission management to developers: a developer can only create roles with permissions that fall within the boundary, preventing privilege escalation. SCPs are the highest-level guardrail in AWS Organizations, applying to every principal in an account (including root) before any IAM evaluation occurs — they define what actions are even possible within an account. The effective permission for any API call is the logical AND (intersection) of all three layers: the identity policy must allow it, the permission boundary must permit it, and no SCP must deny it. A common exam trap is thinking that a generous identity policy can override an SCP — it cannot, because SCPs are evaluated first and an SCP Deny always wins. Another trap: Permission Boundaries do NOT grant permissions; a principal needs both an identity policy and a boundary that allows the action. The management account in an AWS Organization is NOT subject to SCPs, which is why it should be protected with MFA and minimal usage.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: SCPs Don't Grant, Only Restrict
methodSignatures.description: A common mistake is thinking you can use an SCP to grant permissions. SCPs only define what CAN be allowed — actual permissions still must come from IAM identity policies. If an SCP allows s3:*, it does NOT mean everyone in the account has S3 access; they still need an IAM policy granting it.

The canonical Permission Boundary use case: you want developers to create Lambda execution roles, but you don't want them creating a role with AdministratorAccess. Set a boundary that limits new roles to only the services developers need — they can create roles freely but cannot exceed the boundary.

Evaluation order: (1) Deny by default, (2) Check Organizations SCPs, (3) Check resource-based policies, (4) Check IAM permission boundaries, (5) Check session policies, (6) Check identity-based policies. An explicit Deny at ANY step immediately denies the request.

title: Cross-Account Access: Lambda in Account A Accessing DynamoDB in Account B
description: Your company has a microservices architecture across two AWS accounts: Account A (development) hosts a Lambda function, and Account B (production) hosts a DynamoDB table with sensitive customer data. The Lambda in Account A needs to read from the DynamoDB table in Account B without embedding credentials. You need to design the cross-account access pattern.
hints: There is an AWS service that allows one identity to temporarily become another identity and gain different permissions — even across accounts.
Two policies are required: one in Account B to allow Account A to assume a role, and one that defines what permissions that assumed role has.
The Lambda function's execution role needs permission to call a specific STS action.

solution.explanation: Cross-account access in AWS is achieved through IAM Role assumption via AWS Security Token Service (STS). The pattern requires a two-sided trust: Account B creates a role with a trust policy allowing Account A's Lambda execution role as a Principal, and Account A's Lambda execution role must have permission to call sts:AssumeRole on that specific role ARN. At runtime, the Lambda calls STS AssumeRole and receives temporary security credentials (access key, secret key, and session token) that are scoped to only the permissions of the assumed role. This is far more secure than creating an IAM User in Account B and sharing its access keys, because the credentials are temporary and automatically expire. A critical exam point: the trust relationship must be established in BOTH accounts — if either side is missing, the AssumeRole call fails. The ExternalId condition is important for third-party access scenarios (confused deputy problem), though it's less common in internal cross-account setups. The Lambda should cache the assumed credentials and refresh them before expiry rather than calling AssumeRole on every invocation.

methodSignatures.description: Cross-account role assumption requires trust from both sides. Account B's role trust policy must name Account A's role as a trusted Principal, AND Account A's role must have sts:AssumeRole permission on Account B's role ARN. Missing either side will cause AccessDenied.

When a third-party service assumes a role in your account, a malicious actor could trick it into assuming your role for their benefit. Prevent this with an ExternalId condition in the trust policy — only grant assumption when the caller provides a secret ExternalId value you share with the trusted party.

After assuming a cross-account role, the caller's original permissions do NOT apply. Only the assumed role's permissions are active. If the assumed role has dynamodb:GetItem but the Lambda's own role does not, the Lambda can still call GetItem after assuming the role.

title: Enforcing MFA for Sensitive Operations Using IAM Condition Keys
description: A financial services company stores sensitive data in S3 and wants to ensure that even users with S3 delete permissions cannot delete objects unless they have authenticated with MFA during their current session. Developers who have standard S3 read/write access must complete an MFA step before performing any delete operations. You need to design the IAM policy condition.
hints: IAM condition keys can check properties of the authentication session, not just the resource being accessed.
Look at the 'aws:' global condition key namespace — there is a specific key that checks whether MFA was used.
Consider using a Deny statement with a condition that checks if MFA was NOT used, rather than an Allow with MFA required.

solution.explanation: The `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` condition key checks whether the user's session was authenticated with multi-factor authentication during the current session — it returns `true` if MFA was used and `false` (or is absent) if it was not. The recommended approach is to use a Deny statement that fires when MFA is NOT present, rather than an Allow that requires MFA, because explicit Deny always overrides Allow and provides stronger security. Using `BoolIfExists` is the safest operator because it handles both cases: when the key is present and false (user authenticated without MFA), and when the key is absent (session was created via assumed role without MFA context). A subtlety is that for assumed role sessions, `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` may be absent rather than false, which is why `BoolIfExists` or a `Null` condition check is important — using a simple `Bool` operator might miss the absent case. The `aws:MultiFactorAuthAge` key is useful for high-security operations that require recent MFA (e.g., within the last 30 minutes), preventing someone from using an MFA session established hours ago. On the exam, look for scenarios where 'the user has the permission but must prove MFA' — always use `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent` in a Deny condition.

methodSignatures.description: Use BoolIfExists instead of Bool for aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent. The Bool operator only matches if the key EXISTS in the request. BoolIfExists also matches when the key is absent (treating absent as 'false'). Using Bool alone would miss requests where MFA context is entirely absent.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: MFA Age for Time-Sensitive Operations
methodSignatures.description: aws:MultiFactorAuthAge returns the number of seconds since MFA was last authenticated. Use it with NumericLessThan to require fresh MFA: {"NumericGreaterThan": {"aws:MultiFactorAuthAge": "3600"}} in a Deny statement blocks operations if MFA was authenticated more than 1 hour ago.

title: IAM Policy Evaluation: Allow + Deny Conflict Resolution
description: A developer has two IAM policies attached: one allowing full S3 access (s3:*) and another that explicitly denies s3:DeleteObject. Additionally, the developer's IAM Group has a policy allowing s3:DeleteObject on the bucket. The developer tries to delete an object and gets an AccessDenied error despite having two policies that allow deletion.
hints: AWS IAM has a specific evaluation order for Allow and Deny policies — one type always takes priority over the other.
Think about whether having multiple 'Allow' policies for the same action across different policy sources can override an explicit Deny.
The answer involves understanding the absolute rule about explicit Deny statements.

solution.explanation: The IAM policy evaluation model has one absolute rule: an explicit Deny always overrides any Allow, regardless of how many Allow statements exist or where they come from. When Policy 2 explicitly denies `s3:DeleteObject`, that denial is final — AWS does not continue evaluating to find an Allow that might override it. This is different from implicit deny (absence of an Allow), which can be overridden by an Allow statement elsewhere. The developer cannot work around the Deny by adding more Allows; the only fix is to modify or remove the Deny statement itself. This behavior is intentional and is a security feature — it ensures that security-critical denials (like preventing data deletion) cannot be accidentally overridden by another team's permissive policy. On the exam, any scenario with a conflict between Allow and explicit Deny will always resolve to Deny. A common exam trap: 'the user is in a group that allows the action AND has a personal policy that denies it — what is the result?' — always Deny.

methodSignatures.description: Implicit Deny = no Allow statement covers the action (can be fixed with an Allow). Explicit Deny = a policy actively denies the action (can ONLY be fixed by removing or modifying the Deny). Allows can overcome implicit denies but NEVER explicit denies. The exam heavily tests this distinction.

Explicit Deny is checked across ALL policy sources: user policies, group policies, resource-based policies, SCPs, and permission boundaries. If any single policy from any source has an explicit Deny matching the request, access is denied — regardless of Allows in all other policies.

title: Auditing Unused Permissions with IAM Access Analyzer and Credential Reports
description: A security audit reveals that developers in your organization have significantly more permissions than they actually use, violating the principle of least privilege. The CISO wants a systematic approach to identify and remove unused permissions. You need to implement a least privilege audit strategy using AWS native tools without purchasing third-party software.
hints: AWS provides a per-user report showing when credentials (passwords, access keys) were last used.
There is an AWS service that analyzes CloudTrail logs to determine which permissions have actually been used in the last 90 days.
IAM itself provides last-used timestamps for policies, roles, and even individual services within a role.

solution.explanation: AWS provides three complementary native tools for IAM auditing. The IAM Credential Report is a CSV snapshot of all users showing whether their passwords and access keys have been used and when — ideal for identifying completely inactive accounts or unrotated credentials. IAM Access Advisor (now called 'Last Accessed Information') shows which specific AWS services each user or role has permissions to access and when they last used them, powered by CloudTrail — services unused for months are candidates for permission removal. IAM Access Analyzer goes further by continuously analyzing policies to detect resources accessible from outside your account and, with the 'unused access' feature, identifies roles and access keys that haven't been used recently. Using these three tools together enables a systematic least privilege audit: start with Credential Report to find inactive accounts, use Access Advisor to trim service-level permissions from active accounts, and use Access Analyzer for ongoing governance. On the exam, questions about 'identifying unused permissions' or 'implementing least privilege' will typically have IAM Access Advisor as the correct answer for per-user analysis. A common trap is confusing Access Analyzer (finds external access + unused access) with Access Advisor (finds last-accessed service data per identity).

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Access Analyzer vs Access Advisor
methodSignatures.description: Access Advisor = per-user/role tab in IAM showing which services were last accessed (good for per-identity audit). Access Analyzer = account-level service that finds resources shared externally AND unused access patterns (good for continuous governance). Both are different tools — the exam tests knowing which to use when.

The IAM Credential Report takes up to 4 hours to generate if requested too frequently. You must call GenerateCredentialReport first, then GetCredentialReport. It covers all IAM users in the account including root. The report is available in CSV format and shows access key rotation age.

title: Service Control Policies: What SCPs Can and Cannot Do
description: A cloud architect is designing governance for a new AWS Organization with 15 accounts across development, staging, and production OUs. They plan to use Service Control Policies to enforce security baselines such as preventing resource creation outside approved regions, blocking root user actions, and preventing disabling of CloudTrail. A junior developer argues that SCPs can replace IAM policies. You need to clarify what SCPs can and cannot do.
hints: SCPs set the maximum permissions available in an account — think of them as guardrails, not permission grants.
Even a user with AdministratorAccess cannot do something that is explicitly denied by an SCP.
There is one special account in an AWS Organization that behaves differently with SCPs.

solution.explanation: Service Control Policies are organizational guardrails that set the maximum permissions possible within AWS accounts — they define what CAN be allowed, but they do not grant permissions themselves. For a developer to perform an action, two things must both be true: an SCP must not deny it, AND an IAM policy must explicitly allow it. SCPs apply to all principals in member accounts including the root user of those accounts, but critically, they do NOT apply to the management (master) account — this is a major exam point and a real security risk if the management account is compromised. When designing SCPs, you can use a deny list approach (attach FullAWSAccess SCP + add specific deny statements for risky actions) or an allowlist approach (remove FullAWSAccess + attach restrictive allow SCPs). The deny list approach is more practical because it only restricts specific dangerous actions without accidentally blocking legitimate use. A common exam trap is the statement 'SCPs can be used to grant permissions to the root account' — this is false; even the root user in a member account cannot bypass an SCP Deny. Another trap: SCPs do not affect AWS service-linked roles in some cases.

methodSignatures.description: The management (master) account of an AWS Organization is never subject to SCPs. This means root users and IAM entities in the management account can always perform any action regardless of SCPs. For this reason, the management account should be used exclusively for organizational management, with all workloads in member accounts.

SCPs are inherited hierarchically: Root OU → Child OU → Account. An account must have all ancestor SCPs AND its own SCPs allow an action. If the Root OU SCP denies an action, no child OU or account SCP can override that deny. Design SCPs at the highest applicable OU to reduce repetition.

When using SCPs to restrict regions, you must exempt global AWS services that only run in us-east-1: IAM, STS, CloudFront, Route53, AWS Organizations, and Support. Blocking all non-approved regions without exempting these will break IAM logins and certificate management across the entire organization.

title: Black Friday Traffic Spikes: EC2 Pricing and Auto Scaling Strategy
description: An e-commerce company runs its checkout service on EC2. Traffic is steady at 100 requests/second for most of the year, but spikes to 2,000 requests/second on Black Friday and Cyber Monday (a predictable 2-week window). The company wants to minimize costs while ensuring availability during peak periods. They need to choose the right combination of EC2 pricing models and Auto Scaling policies.
hints: The baseline traffic (100 req/sec, year-round) benefits from a commitment-based discount. The spike is predictable, so you know exactly when it will happen.
Auto Scaling has multiple policy types — one is based on schedules (for known peaks), another reacts to current metrics (for unexpected spikes).
Spot Instances are cheapest but can be interrupted — consider whether they are appropriate for checkout (stateful, transactional) workloads.

solution.explanation: The optimal strategy layers different pricing models to match the cost structure to the usage pattern. Reserved Instances or Savings Plans cover the predictable baseline (year-round traffic) at a discount of up to 72% versus On-Demand pricing — this is cost-effective because you know these instances will run continuously. For the predictable Black Friday spike, Scheduled Auto Scaling should pre-provision additional On-Demand instances before traffic arrives, rather than waiting for CloudWatch alarms to trigger — pre-scaling prevents the latency gap between traffic arriving and new instances becoming ready. Target Tracking Scaling provides a safety net for unexpected demand beyond the schedule, maintaining a target metric automatically. Spot Instances are the cheapest option but are inappropriate for the checkout service due to the risk of 2-minute interruption notices during peak payment processing; they are appropriate for background jobs like image processing or report generation. On the exam, the question of which Auto Scaling policy to use for 'predictable patterns' should always lead to Scheduled Scaling as the primary answer, with Target Tracking as a secondary dynamic policy.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Savings Plans vs Reserved Instances
methodSignatures.description: Compute Savings Plans provide up to 66% discount and automatically apply to any EC2 instance type, Lambda, and Fargate in any region — most flexible. EC2 Instance Savings Plans offer up to 72% but lock you to a specific instance family in a specific region. Standard Reserved Instances are similar but can also be sold on the Reserved Instance Marketplace.

After a scaling activity, Auto Scaling waits for the cooldown period (default 300 seconds) before starting another scaling activity. For spiky workloads, reduce the cooldown period. You can also set different cooldowns for scale-out (shorter) and scale-in (longer) to be aggressive about adding capacity but conservative about removing it.

When a Spot Instance is interrupted, AWS gives a 2-minute interruption notice via EC2 instance metadata and EventBridge. Use Spot Instance Interruption Notices to gracefully drain connections, save state, and deregister from load balancers. Spot is best for fault-tolerant, stateless, or checkpointable workloads.

title: Data Loss on EC2 Stop: Instance Store vs EBS
description: A developer builds a stateful web application that caches large amounts of processed data to disk for fast retrieval. The application runs on an EC2 instance that was selected for its very high I/O performance (hundreds of thousands of IOPS). After the EC2 instance is stopped and restarted for patching, all the cached data is gone. The developer is confused because the data was on the 'disk' of the instance.
hints: High-performance I/O EC2 instances (like i3, i4i, d3 families) include a special type of storage that is physically attached to the host machine.
There is a key difference between storage that is 'network-attached' versus storage that is 'local to the physical host'.
Think about what happens to locally attached storage when the virtual machine moves to a different physical host during a stop/start cycle.

solution.explanation: Instance Store provides the highest possible disk I/O performance because the storage is physically attached to the server running the EC2 instance, eliminating network latency. However, this physical attachment means the data is tied to a specific host machine — when an EC2 instance is stopped, it can be moved to a different physical host upon restart, and the original host's storage is not transferred. This makes Instance Store inherently ephemeral. EBS, by contrast, is a network-attached storage service that exists independently of any specific EC2 host — when you stop and start an EC2 instance, the EBS volumes automatically reconnect even if the instance moves to a different physical server. The key distinction that trips up many developers is that rebooting an instance (using the OS reboot command) does NOT move it to a new host, so Instance Store data survives a reboot but is permanently lost on a stop/start cycle. For the exam, any scenario mentioning 'data was lost when the instance was stopped' points to Instance Store, and any scenario requiring 'data persistence across stop/start' requires EBS.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Stop vs Reboot vs Terminate
methodSignatures.description: REBOOT: instance stays on same host, Instance Store preserved, no public IP change. STOP: instance may move to new host, Instance Store LOST, EBS preserved, new public IP on restart (unless Elastic IP). TERMINATE: instance deleted, Instance Store LOST, EBS deleted (unless DeleteOnTermination=false).

methodSignatures.method: Tip: EBS Volume Types for Different Use Cases
methodSignatures.description: gp3: default general purpose, 3000 IOPS baseline, cost-effective. io2: mission-critical databases, up to 256,000 IOPS, 99.999% durability. st1: throughput-optimized HDD for sequential reads (logs, data warehouses). sc1: cold HDD for infrequently accessed data (lowest cost EBS). Choose based on IOPS vs throughput vs cost.

title: Private Subnet EC2 Needs Internet: NAT Gateway Configuration
description: A company deploys its application servers in a private subnet for security — they should not be directly reachable from the internet. However, the EC2 instances need to download software updates, pull Docker images from Docker Hub, and call third-party APIs. A junior developer is confused about how instances in a private subnet can initiate outbound internet connections while remaining inaccessible from the internet.
hints: The solution needs to allow outbound internet connections from private instances while blocking inbound connections from the internet.
This service must be placed in a PUBLIC subnet (not the private subnet) and needs an Elastic IP address.
The private subnet's route table must be updated to direct internet-bound traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to this new service.

solution.explanation: A NAT (Network Address Translation) Gateway allows EC2 instances in private subnets to initiate outbound connections to the internet while preventing the internet from initiating inbound connections to those instances. The NAT Gateway is placed in a public subnet (which has a route to an Internet Gateway) and is assigned an Elastic IP. When a private EC2 instance sends traffic to the internet, it goes to the NAT Gateway first; the Gateway translates the source IP from the private IP to its Elastic IP and forwards the packet to the internet. Response packets come back to the Elastic IP, and the NAT Gateway translates the destination back to the original private IP. This is a one-way NAT — the internet can only respond to connections the private instances initiated, not create new connections to them. For high availability, deploy one NAT Gateway per AZ and update each AZ's private subnet route table to point to its local NAT Gateway; this prevents a single NAT Gateway failure from affecting all private subnets. On the exam, if a private subnet needs internet access, the answer is always NAT Gateway (not Internet Gateway — IGW is for public subnets).

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Internet Gateway vs NAT Gateway
methodSignatures.description: Internet Gateway (IGW): attached to VPC, enables two-way internet communication for instances WITH public IPs (public subnet). NAT Gateway: in public subnet, enables one-way OUTBOUND internet for instances WITHOUT public IPs (private subnet). Private subnet instances NEVER get public IPs — they use NAT GW for internet access.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: NAT Gateway vs NAT Instance Cost
methodSignatures.description: NAT Gateway costs ~$0.045/hour + $0.045/GB processed. NAT Instance costs vary by instance type but can be cheaper for low-traffic scenarios. However, NAT Instance requires you to manage HA, patching, and scaling. The exam almost always prefers NAT Gateway for 'least operational overhead' scenarios.

title: EC2 Pricing Models: Choosing the Right Option Per Scenario
description: A cloud architect needs to advise on EC2 pricing strategies for four different workloads: (1) a production web server running 24/7/365, (2) a development environment used 8 hours/day on weekdays, (3) a big data processing job that can be interrupted and restarted, and (4) an application with unpredictable but significant traffic spikes. Each workload has different availability, cost, and flexibility requirements.
hints: For workloads running 24/7 for more than a year, a commitment-based model gives significant savings over On-Demand.
For workloads that can be interrupted, AWS allows you to bid on unused EC2 capacity at steep discounts.
Development environments that stop overnight benefit from the flexibility of not paying when the instance is stopped.

solution.explanation: EC2 pricing model selection is one of the most frequently tested topics on the DVA-C02 exam. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans are cost-effective only when an instance runs continuously for the commitment period — if a development instance runs only 40 hours per week, a 1-year reservation costs more in amortized cost than On-Demand because you pay for 168 hours per week whether the instance runs or not. Spot Instances offer the greatest savings (up to 90%) by allowing AWS to reclaim the capacity with a 2-minute warning — they are appropriate only for workloads that implement checkpointing and can tolerate interruptions. On-Demand is appropriate as the baseline for unpredictable workloads or short-term needs, and as a supplement to Reserved Instances during demand spikes. Compute Savings Plans are generally more flexible than EC2 Reserved Instances because they automatically apply to any EC2 instance family, region, Lambda, and Fargate — making them preferable when future instance type requirements are uncertain. A common exam trap is choosing Reserved Instances for a development environment that doesn't run 24/7 — always check the actual running hours before recommending commitments.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Break-Even Point for Reserved Instances
methodSignatures.description: On-Demand is cheaper than Reserved if an instance runs less than ~42% of the time (1-year RI break-even). If usage is above ~42% of the month, Reserved starts saving money. For a dev server running 40hrs/week (24% of month), On-Demand is cheaper. Do the math on exam questions: hours_used / total_hours_in_period.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Spot Fleet for High Availability
methodSignatures.description: A single Spot Instance type in one AZ has high interruption risk. Use Spot Fleet with multiple instance types and AZs to increase availability — AWS replaces interrupted instances with available capacity from other pools. Combine with On-Demand instances in the fleet for a guaranteed minimum capacity.

title: EC2 User Data vs Instance Metadata Service (IMDS)
description: A developer is configuring EC2 instances for a new application and needs to understand two commonly confused EC2 features: User Data (for bootstrapping) and the Instance Metadata Service (for runtime instance information). They need to know what each provides, how to access each, and common use cases for both, particularly how applications running on EC2 can discover information about their own environment.
hints: One feature runs scripts BEFORE the application starts (at launch time); the other is a service the running application can query via HTTP.
The runtime metadata service is accessible via a special IP address that is never routable on the internet.
Consider what the difference is between data you GIVE to an instance at launch versus data the instance can DISCOVER about itself.

solution.explanation: EC2 User Data and the Instance Metadata Service serve complementary but distinct purposes. User Data is a bootstrap mechanism — you provide a shell script or cloud-init configuration that runs once when the instance first launches, allowing you to install packages, configure services, and initialize the application without baking everything into a custom AMI. The Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) is a runtime discovery mechanism — it provides a local HTTP endpoint at the non-routable IP 169.254.169.254 that running applications can query to learn about their environment (instance ID, region, IAM credentials) without hardcoding any values. A critical security point is that IMDSv1 is vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks, where a compromised application could be tricked into forwarding requests to IMDS and leaking IAM credentials; IMDSv2 mitigates this by requiring a PUT request to obtain a session token before any metadata can be read. The AWS SDKs automatically use IMDS to retrieve IAM role credentials, which is why applications using IAM roles don't need any credential configuration code. On the exam, if a question asks 'how does the application discover its own instance ID or region at runtime', the answer is IMDS.

methodSignatures.description: Enforce IMDSv2-only by setting HttpTokens=required via the EC2 console, CLI, or launch template. This prevents SSRF attacks where a compromised web app could query IMDS on behalf of an attacker. AWS recommends all new instances use IMDSv2. The AWS SDK v2 uses IMDSv2 by default.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: User Data is NOT Re-run by Default
methodSignatures.description: EC2 User Data runs only at the first boot by default (cloud-init one-time behavior). If you stop and start an instance, User Data does NOT re-run. To run User Data on every boot, add a cloud-init 'scripts-user' module with 'always' run frequency. This is a common exam trap.

title: Security Groups vs NACLs: Stateful vs Stateless Filtering
description: A network security engineer is designing the security architecture for a multi-tier web application with a public web layer and a private database layer. They need to understand when to use Security Groups versus Network ACLs, and a subtle issue arises: a NACL rule was added to allow inbound traffic on port 443, but users are still unable to reach the web server. The engineer needs to diagnose the issue and understand the key behavioral differences between these two security mechanisms.
hints: Security Groups are stateful — they remember the connection state. NACLs are stateless — each packet is evaluated independently.
If inbound traffic is allowed, does a stateless firewall automatically allow the response traffic to go out?
Consider what port the server uses to SEND the response back to the client (it's not port 443 on the server side).

solution.explanation: The issue is that NACLs are stateless — unlike Security Groups, they do not track connection state. When a client sends an HTTPS request to the web server on port 443, the server must respond by sending packets BACK to the client. The response does not come from port 443 on the server; it goes TO an ephemeral (temporary) high-numbered port on the client (typically 1024-65535). The NACL's inbound rule only allowed port 443 inbound, but the outbound response to the client's ephemeral port has no matching NACL outbound rule and is therefore blocked. Security Groups are stateful — they remember that an inbound connection was allowed and automatically permit the response traffic, which is why Security Groups work correctly with just an inbound rule. For NACLs, you must explicitly add outbound rules to allow response traffic using the ephemeral port range. The exam frequently tests this 'stateful vs stateless' distinction — Security Group issues are often about missing inbound rules, while NACL issues are often about missing return traffic rules on ephemeral ports.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Default vs Custom NACL Behavior
methodSignatures.description: The DEFAULT NACL (auto-created with each VPC) allows ALL inbound and outbound traffic. A CUSTOM NACL you create yourself starts with a DENY ALL rule for both inbound and outbound. New developers are often surprised when creating a custom NACL blocks all traffic — you must explicitly add allow rules.

NACLs evaluate rules in ascending order by rule number (100, 110, 120...) and stop at the first match. Place more specific rules first (lower numbers). If you have Allow TCP 443 at rule 100 and Deny TCP 443 at rule 110, port 443 is allowed (100 matches first). Plan rule number spacing to allow future insertion.

title: Zero-Downtime Blue/Green Deployments on EC2
description: A company runs a critical e-commerce application on EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. Deployments currently take the application offline for 10-15 minutes, causing revenue loss. The engineering manager wants to implement blue/green deployments where new code is deployed to a new set of instances and traffic is gradually shifted with the ability to instantly roll back if issues arise.
hints: AWS has a dedicated service for deploying applications to EC2, Lambda, and ECS — it supports multiple deployment strategies including Blue/Green.
In blue/green deployment, 'blue' is the current environment and 'green' is the new environment — traffic must shift between two ALB target groups.
Rollback in blue/green is fast because you simply shift traffic back to the original (blue) environment, which was never terminated.

solution.explanation: AWS CodeDeploy with blue/green deployment strategy provides zero-downtime deployments by maintaining two parallel environments simultaneously. The service provisions a new Auto Scaling Group (green) with the same configuration as the current production group (blue), deploys the new application version to those instances, and then gradually shifts traffic via the Application Load Balancer's target group switching mechanism. The critical advantage of blue/green over in-place deployment is that the original instances remain running and registered with the load balancer during the entire deployment, enabling instant rollback — reverting is just a target group switch that completes in seconds versus a full redeployment that takes minutes. Elastic Beanstalk also offers blue/green via environment URL swapping, but it's a less granular mechanism; CodeDeploy gives more control over traffic shifting increments and validation hooks. The `appspec.yml` file in your code repository defines lifecycle hooks (BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ValidateService) that run scripts to customize the deployment process, such as running database migrations or integration tests before traffic shifts.

methodSignatures.description: CodeDeploy supports: In-Place (rolling, stops instances to update), Blue/Green on EC2 (new ASG, ALB switching), Blue/Green on ECS (task definition replacement), and Canary/Linear/AllAtOnce for Lambda (traffic shifting with aliases). Know which strategy matches which platform on the exam.

The appspec.yml file must be in the ROOT of your application source bundle (not in a subdirectory). For EC2 deployments, it defines files to copy and lifecycle hooks scripts. For Lambda, it defines the function name, alias, and traffic shifting configuration. Missing or malformed appspec.yml is the most common CodeDeploy deployment failure.

title: EC2 Placement Groups: Cluster vs Spread vs Partition
description: A company is designing EC2 infrastructure for three different workloads: (1) a high-performance computing (HPC) cluster that requires sub-millisecond network latency between nodes for parallel processing, (2) a critical database cluster of 7 nodes where they need hardware failure isolation guarantees, and (3) a distributed big data application with 48 instances that processes data in parallel across multiple racks for fault tolerance at scale.
hints: One placement group type packs all instances onto the same physical rack/host for maximum network performance — great for performance but terrible for fault isolation.
One type ensures each instance is on a completely different rack — maximum isolation but limits scale.
One type lets you define logical 'partitions' where each partition is isolated to its own rack — useful for large distributed systems.

solution.explanation: Placement Groups control the physical placement of EC2 instances on underlying hardware to optimize for either performance or fault tolerance. Cluster Placement Groups co-locate all instances on the same physical rack within a single AZ, enabling 10+ Gbps network throughput and sub-millisecond latency ideal for HPC and ML training — but this performance comes at the cost of correlated failure risk (rack outage = all instances down). Spread Placement Groups guarantee each instance is on separate physical hardware (different rack, power, and network), providing maximum isolation, but are strictly limited to 7 instances per AZ — making them appropriate only for small critical clusters like a primary/replica database pair. Partition Placement Groups bridge the gap for large-scale distributed systems: they partition hundreds of instances into logical groups where each partition is rack-isolated from others, but instances within a partition may share hardware. Applications like HDFS and Cassandra can use the partition metadata from IMDS to ensure data replicas are stored on instances in different partitions, guaranteeing that a single rack failure never destroys all replicas. On the exam, the Spread limit of 7 per AZ is frequently tested — if a scenario has more than 7 instances that need isolation, the answer is Partition, not Spread.

methodSignatures.description: Spread Placement Groups allow a maximum of 7 running instances per AZ. This is a hard limit, not a soft limit. If you need more than 7 isolated instances in an AZ, use Partition Placement Groups instead. Exam questions often use numbers like '10 critical instances' as a trap to see if you know this limit.

When launching instances into a Cluster Placement Group, launch all instances at once using a single request. If you launch some now and add more later, AWS may not have capacity on the same rack and will return an InsufficientInstanceCapacity error. It's a good practice to launch with more instances than needed and stop the extras.

title: Automating Log Storage Cost Reduction with S3 Lifecycle Policies
description: A company stores application logs in S3. Logs from the last 7 days are frequently accessed for debugging; logs from 7-30 days are occasionally queried; logs from 30-90 days are rarely accessed but must be retrievable within hours; logs older than 90 days need to be archived but are almost never accessed and retrieval within 12 hours is acceptable; logs older than 365 days can be deleted. The team wants this tiering to happen automatically.
hints: S3 has multiple storage classes optimized for different access frequencies, from millisecond to hour-long retrieval times.
S3 Lifecycle Policies can automatically transition objects between storage classes and expire (delete) objects based on their age.
Glacier classes have retrieval time tradeoffs — Instant Retrieval is seconds, Flexible Retrieval is minutes to hours, Deep Archive is up to 12 hours.

solution.explanation: S3 Lifecycle Policies enable fully automated tiered storage management by defining rules that transition objects between storage classes based on object age. The storage class hierarchy trades retrieval speed and retrieval cost for lower storage cost as data ages: Standard offers instant access with no retrieval fee at the highest storage cost; Standard-IA cuts storage costs by ~58% but adds a per-GB retrieval fee for data that isn't accessed regularly; Glacier Instant Retrieval provides similar access speed to Standard-IA at even lower storage costs with higher retrieval fees; Glacier Flexible Retrieval reduces storage costs further at the expense of minutes-to-hours retrieval time. A critical operational consideration is minimum storage duration: Standard-IA objects are charged for a minimum of 30 days even if deleted sooner — so transitioning objects before 30 days to Standard-IA will not save money. The exam frequently tests knowing when to use Intelligent-Tiering (unknown access patterns, avoids retrieval fees by keeping frequently accessed objects in Standard tier automatically) versus manual lifecycle rules (known, predictable access patterns). For log files with well-known aging patterns, manual lifecycle rules are more cost-effective than Intelligent-Tiering because they avoid the per-object monitoring fee.

methodSignatures.description: S3 charges minimum storage durations regardless of when you delete: Standard-IA = 30 days, Glacier Instant Retrieval = 90 days, Glacier Flexible = 90 days, Glacier Deep Archive = 180 days. If you delete or transition an object earlier, you're still billed for the minimum. Factor this into your cost analysis for short-lived objects.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Glacier Restore vs Direct Access
methodSignatures.description: Glacier Flexible Retrieval objects cannot be directly read — you must submit a Restore request first, which creates a temporary copy in S3 Standard for a specified number of days (1-30). Glacier Instant Retrieval is an exception: it supports millisecond retrieval without a separate restore step, making it suitable for archives that still need to be occasionally accessed immediately.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: S3 Intelligent-Tiering for Unknown Patterns
methodSignatures.description: S3 Intelligent-Tiering monitors access patterns and automatically moves objects between Frequent Access, Infrequent Access, and Archive tiers. It has no retrieval fee (unlike Standard-IA) but charges a small per-object monitoring fee (~$0.0025 per 1,000 objects/month). Best for unpredictable or evolving access patterns; not cost-effective for very small objects or predictable patterns.

title: Direct Browser Uploads to S3 Using Presigned URLs
description: A photo-sharing application allows users to upload images directly from their browser. Currently uploads go through the application server (EC2), which proxies them to S3 — this wastes bandwidth, increases server load, and slows uploads. The team wants users to upload files directly to S3 from the browser without exposing AWS credentials and without allowing users to upload to arbitrary locations.
hints: AWS allows you to generate a URL that includes authentication information embedded in the URL itself — the URL is only valid for a limited time period.
This mechanism is generated server-side using your AWS credentials and grants temporary, scoped access to a specific S3 object or prefix.
For browser uploads (POST method), there is a specific form of this mechanism that includes a policy document.

solution.explanation: S3 Presigned URLs solve the problem of granting temporary, scoped access to S3 without exposing long-term credentials. The server-side application generates a URL that cryptographically embeds the authorization (derived from the server's IAM credentials), the specific S3 object path, and an expiry timestamp. When the browser sends a PUT request to this URL, S3 validates the signature and allows the upload only if the URL hasn't expired and the content matches any embedded conditions. This offloads the data transfer from your application servers entirely — the upload goes directly from the user's browser to S3, reducing server bandwidth costs and latency. A subtle but exam-critical point: the presigned URL's validity is tied to the signer's credentials — if the IAM Role's temporary credentials (valid for ~1-6 hours) expire before the presigned URL's stated expiry, the URL will fail with an authentication error before its intended expiry. For HTML form-based uploads, Presigned POST is preferable because it includes a policy document that can enforce file size limits and content type restrictions server-side, preventing users from uploading unexpected content even with a valid presigned URL.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Presigned URL Expiry with Assumed Roles
methodSignatures.description: When a Lambda function (using an assumed IAM Role) generates a presigned URL, the URL's effective expiry is the MINIMUM of: (a) the specified expiry time, and (b) the remaining validity of the role's session token (default 1 hour). Always factor role credential lifetime into presigned URL expiry design.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Presigned URL vs Bucket Policy Public Access
methodSignatures.description: Presigned URLs allow access to objects without making the bucket public. The URL acts as a temporary, per-object, time-limited access grant. This is far more secure than setting a bucket to public-read. Use presigned URLs for any user-specific content delivery; use CloudFront signed URLs/cookies for large-scale content distribution.

title: S3 Replication: CRR vs SRR — Requirements and Use Cases
description: A company wants to replicate S3 objects for two different purposes: (1) replicate objects to another AWS region for disaster recovery and compliance (data must exist in EU and US regions), and (2) replicate objects within the same region to a separate bucket used by their analytics team. A developer needs to understand the requirements for enabling replication and which replication type applies to each use case.
hints: Replication in S3 requires a feature that tracks object versions — without it, S3 cannot determine which objects need to be replicated.
Replication is not retroactive — only new objects created after the replication rule is enabled are automatically replicated.
Think about whether existing objects before enabling replication are covered, and what special one-time operation exists for them.

solution.explanation: S3 replication requires versioning to be enabled on both the source and destination buckets because replication works by tracking object versions — without versioning, S3 has no mechanism to identify new or changed objects that need to be replicated. This mandatory prerequisite is the most commonly tested fact about S3 replication on the exam. Cross-Region Replication (CRR) is the appropriate choice for disaster recovery and compliance scenarios requiring geographic separation of data, while Same-Region Replication (SRR) serves use cases like creating a separate analytics copy without data egress costs. A critical operational point is that replication is NOT retroactive — enabling a replication rule will not copy objects that already existed in the bucket; you must use S3 Batch Replication or AWS CLI sync for existing objects. By default, delete operations (adding a delete marker) are NOT replicated — if a user deletes an object in the source, the replica is not deleted, which provides accidental deletion protection. Replication also does not automatically replicate objects in Glacier — you cannot replicate objects that have been transitioned to cold storage tiers.

methodSignatures.description: By default, when you delete an object in the source bucket (adding a delete marker), the delete marker is NOT replicated to the destination. This protects against accidental mass-deletion propagating to your replica. You can optionally enable delete marker replication in the replication rule if you want deletions to propagate.

S3 replication supports SSE-S3 and SSE-KMS encrypted objects. For SSE-KMS objects, you must specify a KMS key for the destination region and give the replication IAM role permission to use both the source and destination KMS keys. SSE-C (customer-provided keys) objects cannot be replicated.

title: Restricting S3 Bucket Access to a Specific VPC
description: A company stores sensitive financial data in S3. A security audit requires that the data must ONLY be accessible from within the company's internal VPC — all access from the public internet must be blocked, even from users with valid IAM credentials. The application servers in the VPC need seamless access without going through the public internet, which also saves data transfer costs.
hints: AWS has a service that creates a private gateway endpoint within your VPC, allowing VPC resources to access S3 without internet routing.
S3 bucket policies support condition keys that check which VPC endpoint or which VPC the request is coming from.
The bucket policy must explicitly deny requests that do NOT come through the approved VPC endpoint.

solution.explanation: Restricting S3 access to a specific VPC requires two components working together: a VPC Gateway Endpoint that creates a private network path from the VPC to S3, and an S3 bucket policy that denies any requests not originating from that specific endpoint. The VPC Gateway Endpoint adds an entry to the VPC's route table directing S3-bound traffic through the private AWS backbone instead of the internet gateway, eliminating data transfer costs and ensuring traffic never leaves the AWS network. The bucket policy uses the `aws:SourceVpce` condition key to check whether the request arrived through the approved endpoint, and denies all other requests — including requests from IAM users with valid credentials who are accessing from outside the VPC (e.g., from their laptop). A subtle but important point: the Deny policy must use `Principal: *` (all principals) to cover all access, not just unauthenticated access. Gateway Endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free, unlike Interface Endpoints (PrivateLink) which charge per hour plus data; for same-region S3 access, Gateway Endpoints are always the more cost-effective choice. On the exam, VPC Endpoint + bucket policy is the correct answer for 'access S3 only from within VPC' scenarios.

methodSignatures.description: Gateway Endpoint: free, only for S3 and DynamoDB, works within same region, modifies route tables, no DNS changes. Interface Endpoint (PrivateLink): charged, works for all AWS services, supports cross-region and on-premises (via DX/VPN), uses private DNS. For S3 in same region, Gateway is always cheaper and simpler.

VPC Endpoints have their own policy (endpoint policy) that acts as an additional access control layer. The endpoint policy controls which S3 buckets can be accessed via this endpoint. Combined with the bucket policy (which checks the endpoint ID), you get bidirectional control: endpoint decides which buckets you can reach, bucket decides which endpoints can access it.

title: S3 Static Website 403 Errors: Diagnosis and Fixes
description: A developer hosts a static website on S3 with static website hosting enabled. The website URL returns 403 Forbidden errors. When they try to fix it by making the bucket public, they still get errors. The developer is confused because the bucket policy looks correct and the files are definitely in the bucket. They need to systematically diagnose all possible causes of 403 errors on S3 static websites.
hints: There is an account-level and bucket-level setting in S3 that can override bucket policies and prevent public access regardless of the policy content.
CORS errors (different from 403) occur when a browser script from one domain tries to load resources from another domain — this is a distinct issue from 403.
The 403 error on a static website can also appear if the specific file being requested does not exist (S3 returns 403 for missing files on public buckets, not 404).

solution.explanation: The most common cause of 403 errors on new S3 static websites is the Block Public Access settings, which AWS enables by default on all new buckets and accounts as a security best practice. These settings can override even a correctly written bucket policy — if `RestrictPublicBuckets` is enabled at the account level, no amount of bucket policy configuration will make the bucket publicly accessible. After confirming Block Public Access is disabled, the next check is the bucket policy itself — the most common policy mistake is setting the Resource to the bucket ARN (`arn:aws:s3:::bucket-name`) without the `/*` suffix, which grants permission to list the bucket but not to retrieve individual objects. S3 returns 403 (not 404) for missing objects in non-public buckets as a security measure to prevent enumeration of object keys, which confuses developers into thinking the issue is a permissions problem when the file simply doesn't exist. CORS configuration is a separate concern — it doesn't cause 403 in the HTTP status code sense but can cause browser-level fetch errors that look like permission issues in the developer console. The static website hosting endpoint only supports HTTP (not HTTPS); for HTTPS, you must use CloudFront in front of S3.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Block Public Access Default State
methodSignatures.description: Since April 2023, all new S3 buckets have Block Public Access enabled by default at both the account and bucket level. Any new bucket policy attempting to grant public access will be ignored until BPA is explicitly disabled. Always check BPA settings first when debugging 'bucket policy seems correct but still 403' issues.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Static Website vs REST Endpoint
methodSignatures.description: S3 static website hosting endpoint (http://bucket.s3-website-region.amazonaws.com) and the REST API endpoint (https://bucket.s3.region.amazonaws.com) behave differently: static website supports index documents, error documents, and redirects but requires public access; REST endpoint supports HTTPS and presigned URLs but doesn't support web browser redirect rules.

title: S3 Event Notifications: Building a Thumbnail Generation Pipeline
description: A media company wants to automatically generate thumbnail images whenever a user uploads a new photo to an S3 bucket. The system should trigger image processing immediately upon upload, support high-volume concurrent uploads, and integrate with the existing notification infrastructure (some teams need email alerts for new uploads, others need queue-based processing). You need to design the S3 event notification architecture.
hints: S3 Event Notifications support three direct targets and one indirect routing service.
For fan-out (one event reaching multiple destinations), there is a pattern using SNS to distribute to multiple SQS queues and Lambda functions.
EventBridge (CloudWatch Events) offers a more flexible alternative to S3 Event Notifications with more filtering capabilities.

solution.explanation: S3 Event Notifications provide three direct integration targets: Lambda (for immediate processing), SQS (for decoupled queue-based processing), and SNS (for pub/sub fan-out to multiple subscribers). For the thumbnail generation use case, the fan-out pattern using SNS as the S3 destination is the cleanest architecture — S3 sends one notification to SNS, which then distributes it to all subscribers simultaneously (Lambda for thumbnail generation, SQS for downstream services, email for admin alerts). EventBridge is an increasingly preferred alternative for complex routing scenarios because it supports more target types, content-based filtering, event archiving, and replay capabilities. An important limitation is that S3 Event Notifications only support Standard SQS queues, not FIFO queues — if strict ordering is required, EventBridge with a FIFO consumer is necessary. S3 Event Notifications are 'at least once' delivery, meaning your processing logic should be idempotent (processing the same event twice should not cause data corruption). The S3 event payload includes the bucket name, object key, size, ETag, and event type, giving Lambda enough information to process the new file.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: S3 Notification vs EventBridge Comparison
methodSignatures.description: S3 Event Notifications: simpler, lower latency, directly configured on bucket, limited filtering (prefix/suffix only), limited targets (Lambda/SQS/SNS). EventBridge: requires enabling S3→EventBridge forwarding, richer content-based filtering (object size, storage class), more targets, supports archive/replay. Choose EventBridge for complex multi-destination routing.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Idempotent Processing for S3 Events
methodSignatures.description: S3 Event Notifications guarantee at-least-once delivery. Your Lambda function or SQS consumer may receive the same event multiple times (duplicate notifications). Design processing to be idempotent: check if thumbnail already exists before generating, use conditional writes, or use the object ETag as a deduplication key.

title: S3 Versioning and MFA Delete: Protection Against Accidental Deletion
description: A company accidentally deleted critical application configuration files from S3. After investigation, they discover S3 versioning was not enabled. They now want to enable versioning and add an extra layer of protection (MFA Delete) to prevent accidental or malicious deletion of S3 object versions. A developer asks about costs, how to restore deleted objects, and what MFA Delete actually protects.
hints: When you 'delete' a versioned object, S3 doesn't actually remove the data — it adds a special marker instead.
To recover a 'deleted' versioned object, you need to interact with the specific version ID, not the current 'deleted' state.
MFA Delete requires the bucket owner to provide an MFA code to permanently delete a specific version or change the versioning state.

solution.explanation: S3 Versioning protects against accidental deletion and overwrites by preserving all versions of an object — a 'deleted' versioned object is not actually removed; instead, a delete marker is placed over the current version, making it appear deleted to standard requests while keeping all version data intact and recoverable. To restore such an object, you simply delete the delete marker (not the object itself), which causes the most recent actual version to become current again. MFA Delete adds a second authentication factor requirement specifically for the irreversible operations: permanently deleting a specific version or changing the versioning configuration. This means that even if an attacker gains access to an IAM user's credentials, they cannot permanently destroy version history without also possessing the physical MFA device. A significant operational concern with versioning is storage cost: every version is stored as a complete copy of the object, and all versions persist until explicitly removed — for frequently modified or large objects, this can multiply storage costs significantly. Lifecycle rules should always be created alongside versioning enablement to automatically expire non-current versions after a configurable retention period.

methodSignatures.description: MFA Delete can ONLY be enabled by the bucket owner using the ROOT account credentials (not IAM users, even with full S3 access). It must be configured via AWS CLI or SDK, not the console. This is intentional — if IAM credentials are compromised, an attacker cannot simply enable/disable MFA Delete through the console.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Versioning Cost Control with Lifecycle
methodSignatures.description: Enable versioning and then immediately create lifecycle rules: (1) NoncurrentVersionTransition — move old versions to cheaper storage (Glacier) after 30 days, (2) NoncurrentVersionExpiration — delete old versions after 90 days, (3) ExpiredObjectDeleteMarker — clean up orphaned delete markers to reduce storage noise.

title: S3 Encryption Options: SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, SSE-C, and Client-Side
description: A healthcare company needs to store patient records in S3 in compliance with HIPAA. Different data types have different security requirements: some need automatic encryption with AWS managing all key operations, some need an audit trail of every encryption/decryption operation for compliance, and some data is so sensitive that the company insists on managing the encryption keys entirely outside AWS. The security team needs to choose the right encryption approach for each use case.
hints: One option uses AWS-managed keys where you never interact with keys directly — AWS handles all key management transparently.
One option uses AWS Key Management Service where you can control key policies, enable key rotation, and see CloudTrail logs for every use of the key.
One option requires the client to provide the encryption key with EVERY request — AWS uses the key to encrypt/decrypt but never stores it.

solution.explanation: S3 server-side encryption options represent a spectrum of key control and auditability. SSE-S3 is the simplest option — AWS fully manages all key operations with no customer visibility into individual key use, making it appropriate for data requiring encryption but not a detailed cryptographic audit trail. SSE-KMS shifts key management to AWS Key Management Service, where you control the key policy and every encryption/decryption operation generates a CloudTrail API event with the identity of the requester, the key used, and the timestamp — this audit trail is what makes SSE-KMS appropriate for HIPAA, PCI-DSS, and other compliance frameworks. SSE-C provides maximum key isolation — the customer provides a unique key with each request, AWS uses it transiently, and then discards it, meaning AWS can never decrypt the data without the customer actively providing the key — however, this places the entire burden of key security and management on the customer. The KMS API throttling limit is an important operational concern for high-throughput S3 workloads — using an S3 Bucket Key reduces the number of KMS API calls from one per object to one per bucket key generation period, significantly reducing costs and throttling risk for SSE-KMS.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: S3 Bucket Keys Reduce KMS Costs
methodSignatures.description: By default, SSE-KMS calls KMS for every S3 object operation (encrypt/decrypt). Enable S3 Bucket Keys to generate a bucket-level data key from KMS, then use that to encrypt individual objects — this reduces KMS API call volume by up to 99% and can dramatically reduce costs for buckets with millions of objects.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: KMS Key Types for S3
methodSignatures.description: Three KMS key types with S3: (1) S3-managed KMS key (aws/s3): AWS-owned, free, no key policy control, no cross-account use. (2) AWS-managed CMK: per-service, viewable in KMS, some control, no cross-account. (3) Customer-managed CMK: full control, key policy, rotation, cross-account use, most expensive. HIPAA/compliance usually requires Customer-managed CMK for auditability.

title: Lambda Timeout Processing Large S3 Files
description: A Lambda function is triggered by S3 ObjectCreated events and processes large video metadata files (2-8 GB each). The function is hitting the 15-minute Lambda timeout limit and failing to process the largest files. The team needs a solution that handles arbitrarily large files reliably, with proper error handling and the ability to retry failed files.
hints: Lambda has a hard maximum timeout of 15 minutes — no configuration can extend this. Think about what other compute options exist for longer-running tasks.
S3 supports reading only a specific byte range of an object — you could split the processing into multiple smaller Lambda invocations each handling a chunk.
An asynchronous queue-based approach can decouple the S3 event trigger from the actual processing, allowing a different compute type to handle long jobs.

solution.explanation: Lambda's 15-minute hard timeout is a fundamental constraint that cannot be configured away — it's a deliberate design choice to keep Lambda functions focused and stateless. When files are too large to process within this limit, the solution depends on whether the file's data can be processed in independent chunks. S3 Byte-Range reads allow Lambda to retrieve specific sections of a file using HTTP Range headers, enabling parallel processing where multiple Lambda invocations each handle a portion of the file simultaneously, dramatically reducing wall-clock time. For jobs that inherently require sequential processing beyond 15 minutes, SQS decoupling is the cleanest pattern: Lambda quickly enqueues a job reference (the S3 key) into SQS, and a long-running compute target (EC2, ECS, or Fargate) polls the queue and processes the file without any timeout constraint. AWS Fargate is the serverless option for long-running container tasks — it eliminates server management while allowing processing jobs that run for hours. Step Functions adds orchestration logic, retry handling, and parallel processing coordination on top of any of these compute types.

methodSignatures.description: Set Lambda timeout to the 99th percentile of expected execution time + buffer, NOT the maximum 15 minutes. An oversized timeout means failures wait longer before being retried. Set CloudWatch Alarms on Lambda Duration metrics to detect timeout trends before they become production incidents.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: /tmp Storage for Large Intermediate Files
methodSignatures.description: Lambda's /tmp directory provides 512 MB to 10,240 MB of ephemeral disk storage (configurable). Use it for intermediate files during processing (e.g., downloading a file chunk, processing it, uploading results). /tmp contents are NOT cleared between warm invocations — clear explicitly or use random filenames to avoid stale data across invocations.

title: Lambda Cold Start Latency: Solutions and Tradeoffs
description: A production API backed by Lambda functions is experiencing occasional high-latency responses (3-4 seconds) on the first request after periods of inactivity. Users are complaining about slow initial loads. The application is a customer-facing web API where P99 latency must be under 500ms. The team needs to understand Lambda cold starts and evaluate the available solutions.
hints: Lambda must create a new execution environment (download code, initialize runtime, run initialization code) before the first invocation — this initialization time is the cold start.
AWS offers a feature that pre-warms Lambda execution environments at a cost — so they are always ready to handle requests without initialization delay.
For Java runtimes specifically, AWS offers a snapshot-based optimization that dramatically reduces cold start times.

solution.explanation: Lambda cold starts occur because AWS must provision a new execution environment from scratch when no warm environment is available — this includes downloading and unpacking the deployment package, starting the runtime process, and executing any initialization code outside the handler function. Python and Node.js cold starts typically take 100-500ms while Java cold starts (due to JVM startup) can take 1-10 seconds. Provisioned Concurrency is the definitive solution: it pre-initializes a specified number of execution environments that are kept warm and ready, completely eliminating cold start latency for those concurrent requests. It must be applied to a published Lambda version or alias (not `$LATEST`) and incurs per-environment-per-hour charges even when not receiving traffic. Lambda SnapStart for Java works differently — instead of keeping environments running, it snapshots the fully initialized execution environment and restores from that snapshot on demand, achieving near-instant cold starts while only paying for the snapshot storage. The common 'keep-warm' pattern of pinging Lambda every 5 minutes is unreliable because traffic spikes exceeding the single warm environment still trigger cold starts — Provisioned Concurrency is the production-grade solution.

methodSignatures.description: These are often confused: PROVISIONED Concurrency = pre-warms execution environments (eliminates cold starts, costs money even with no traffic). RESERVED Concurrency = limits maximum concurrent executions for a function (prevents one function from consuming all account concurrency, does NOT prevent cold starts and does NOT pre-warm anything).

SnapStart snapshots the execution environment after the init phase. If your init code creates unique state (unique IDs, network connections, seeded random values), you must use the beforeCheckpoint hook to clean state before snapshotting, and afterRestore hook to re-initialize unique state after restoration. Failing to do this can cause multiple functions to share the same 'unique' IDs.

title: Lambda in VPC: Accessing RDS in a Private Subnet
description: A Lambda function needs to query an RDS PostgreSQL database that resides in a private subnet of a VPC. The function currently fails with a connection timeout error. A developer has configured the Lambda function to run inside the VPC (assigned it to the private subnet), but the function still cannot connect to RDS. Additionally, after placing Lambda in the VPC, the function can no longer call external APIs on the internet.
hints: Even when Lambda is in the same VPC as RDS, a Security Group on the RDS instance must explicitly allow inbound connections from the Lambda function's Security Group.
Lambda functions in a VPC behave like EC2 instances in that VPC — if the subnet is private (no NAT Gateway), there is no internet access.
For Lambda functions making many short-lived connections to RDS, there is a managed proxy service that prevents connection pool exhaustion.

solution.explanation: Placing Lambda inside a VPC does not automatically grant it access to resources in that VPC — Security Groups still control all traffic and must be explicitly configured to allow Lambda to connect to RDS. The RDS Security Group must have an inbound rule allowing traffic from the Lambda function's Security Group on the database port; using Security Group references (rather than IP ranges) is best practice for dynamic Lambda networking. A commonly misunderstood behavior is that Lambda functions in a VPC — even in a public subnet — cannot access the internet because Lambda ENIs are not assigned public IP addresses; internet access from VPC-attached Lambda requires routing through a NAT Gateway. At scale, Lambda functions create a new database connection per invocation, which can quickly exhaust RDS's connection pool — RDS Proxy solves this by acting as a connection multiplexer, maintaining a pool of long-lived RDS connections and routing many Lambda invocations through that shared pool. RDS Proxy also improves failover speed for Multi-AZ RDS from 20-40 seconds to under 5 seconds by caching the DNS endpoint.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Lambda VPC Network Interface Creation
methodSignatures.description: When Lambda is assigned to a VPC, it creates Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs) in the specified subnets. This process used to cause cold starts (ENI creation takes time), but AWS introduced Hyperplane ENIs in 2020 — Lambda now pre-creates ENIs per subnet/SG combination and shares them across functions, eliminating the ENI creation cold start.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: RDS Proxy Authentication via IAM
methodSignatures.description: RDS Proxy supports IAM authentication — Lambda can authenticate to the proxy using its IAM role (via RDS generate-db-auth-token) instead of storing database passwords. Combined with Secrets Manager for the proxy-to-RDS password, this creates a fully credential-free connection chain for Lambda → RDS Proxy → RDS.

title: Lambda Concurrency Limits: Reserved vs Provisioned Concurrency and Throttling
description: A company's Lambda function is processing real-time payment transactions and suddenly starts receiving throttling errors (429 Too Many Requests). The function is hitting the account-level concurrency limit of 1,000. Simultaneously, another critical Lambda function handling user authentication is also being throttled because the payment function is consuming the entire concurrency pool. The team needs to fix this and prevent future incidents.
hints: AWS allows you to guarantee a specific amount of concurrency for a function, preventing it from being starved by other functions in the account.
The same feature that guarantees concurrency for one function also limits that function from consuming more than its reserved amount.
When a synchronously invoked Lambda is throttled, the error propagates back to the caller. When an asynchronously invoked Lambda is throttled, AWS has a built-in retry mechanism.

solution.explanation: Lambda concurrency management requires understanding the interplay between the account-level pool and per-function controls. By default, all Lambda functions in an account share a single concurrency pool — a burst in one function can starve all others. Reserved Concurrency solves this dual-purpose problem: it both guarantees a function will always have access to its reserved amount AND caps the function at that limit, preventing any single function from monopolizing the shared pool.
