Setting Reserved Concurrency for critical functions like authentication is essential architectural practice — without it, high-traffic functions will crowd out critical low-traffic ones during peak periods. The throttling behavior difference between synchronous and asynchronous invocations is a common exam topic: synchronous calls (API Gateway → Lambda) return 429 immediately to the caller who must handle retries; asynchronous invocations are automatically retried by Lambda's internal queue for up to 6 hours, providing built-in durability. Provisioned Concurrency is orthogonal to Reserved Concurrency — a function can have both (Reserved for quota guarantee, Provisioned for cold start elimination) or either independently.

methodSignatures.description: Lambda has an initial burst limit per region (500-3,000 concurrent executions depending on region). Beyond the burst limit, concurrency scales at 500 additional executions per minute. If traffic grows faster than this ramp rate, throttling occurs even if you're under the account limit. Provisioned Concurrency is the only way to handle instant traffic spikes beyond the burst limit.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Reserved Concurrency = 0 as Circuit Breaker
methodSignatures.description: Setting a Lambda function's Reserved Concurrency to 0 is a useful operational tool — it immediately stops all invocations of that function (they're all throttled). This acts as a circuit breaker to quickly disable a misbehaving function without deleting or redeploying it. Useful during incident response.

title: Lambda Event Source Mapping: SQS, Kinesis, and DynamoDB Streams
description: A developer is integrating Lambda with three different event sources: an SQS Standard queue for order processing, a Kinesis Data Stream for real-time clickstream analytics, and a DynamoDB Stream for change data capture. They need to understand how batching works for each, how errors are handled differently, and how to prevent a single bad message from blocking all processing.
hints: SQS messages within a batch are independent — a failed message can be handled by reporting partial batch failures without failing the entire batch.
Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams are ordered shards — if one record fails, the shard is blocked until the error is resolved (stream position doesn't advance).
There is a feature that splits a failing batch in half to identify which specific record is causing the failure, preventing a bad message from blocking the entire shard.

solution.explanation: Lambda event source mapping works differently for SQS (pull-based, message queue) versus Kinesis/DynamoDB Streams (pull-based, ordered streams). For SQS, messages are independent and the partial batch failure feature allows Lambda to report individual message failures — only the reported failed messages are returned to the queue while successful ones are deleted, preventing unnecessary reprocessing. For Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams, records within a shard are strictly ordered, and a processing failure causes Lambda to retry the same batch repeatedly until it succeeds or the records expire — this can cause a single corrupted record (poison pill) to completely block all subsequent records in the shard for the entire retention period. The Bisect on Error feature addresses this: when enabled and a batch fails, Lambda automatically splits the batch in half and retries each half separately, recursively narrowing down to the specific failing record(s). Once isolated, the bad record can be sent to a failure destination (SQS DLQ or S3) and normal processing resumes. Filter criteria can also help by preventing Lambda from even receiving events that match known bad patterns.

methodSignatures.description: Set SQS visibility timeout to AT LEAST 6x the Lambda timeout. If Lambda timeout is 5 minutes, set visibility timeout to 30 minutes. If Lambda fails midway and the visibility timeout expires before failure is reported, the message becomes visible and another Lambda picks it up — causing duplicate processing.

Standard Kinesis consumer (Lambda event source mapping) uses shared 2 MB/sec throughput across all consumers of a shard. Enhanced Fan-Out gives each Lambda consumer its own dedicated 2 MB/sec via a push-based subscription — better for high-throughput scenarios with multiple Lambda consumers reading from the same shard.

title: Lambda Layers: Shared Libraries and Custom Runtimes
description: A development team has five Lambda functions that all depend on the same set of third-party libraries (NumPy, Pandas, a custom internal library) totaling 150 MB. Currently, these libraries are bundled into each function's deployment package, resulting in 5 identical 150 MB bundles totaling 750 MB of redundant storage and slow deployments. They need a better approach to share common dependencies across functions.
hints: Lambda Layers allow you to package and share code or dependencies as a separate artifact that multiple Lambda functions can reference.
When a Lambda function uses a Layer, the layer's contents are extracted to a standard path in the function's execution environment.
Lambda Layers can also contain non-library content like custom runtimes for languages not natively supported by Lambda.

solution.explanation: Lambda Layers solve the dependency duplication problem by allowing teams to package shared libraries and code as separate versioned ZIP archives that are mounted into Lambda execution environments at the standard `/opt` path. Instead of bundling 150 MB of libraries into every deployment package, you create one layer containing those libraries and reference it by ARN from each function — the layer content is provided automatically at execution time without being included in the function's ZIP. This dramatically speeds up deployments (only the small function code ZIP is uploaded on code changes), reduces storage costs, and centralizes library version management (updating one layer propagates to all referencing functions upon alias/version update). Lambda Layers are also the mechanism for custom runtimes — by including a `bootstrap` executable in the layer that implements the Lambda runtime API protocol, you can run Lambda in any language (even compiled languages not natively supported). The 250 MB total unzipped limit across all layers plus function code is the critical constraint; container images (up to 10 GB) are the alternative for large ML models or comprehensive data science environments.

methodSignatures.description: Lambda functions reference a layer by its full versioned ARN (e.g., arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789:layer:MyLayer:5). Functions keep using the pinned version until explicitly updated — a new layer version does NOT automatically apply to referencing functions. This prevents unexpected dependency updates from breaking production functions.

Lambda container images (up to 10 GB) include all dependencies in the image itself — layers are irrelevant for container-based Lambda. Use container images when total package size exceeds 250 MB, when you need a specific OS/runtime configuration, or when using ML models. Lambda container images support Docker and must implement the Lambda Runtime Interface.

title: Lambda Configuration Management: Env Vars vs Parameter Store vs Secrets Manager
description: A Lambda function needs access to three types of configuration: (1) a non-sensitive database endpoint hostname that is different per environment (dev/staging/prod), (2) an API feature flag that changes frequently (multiple times per day) and needs to be updated without redeploying Lambda, and (3) a database password that must be automatically rotated every 30 days and kept encrypted. You need to choose the right configuration storage mechanism for each.
hints: Lambda Environment Variables are baked into the deployment package and require a function update (redeployment) when they change.
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store and Secrets Manager are external services accessed via API — changes take effect without redeploying Lambda.
Secrets Manager has a specific feature for automatically rotating credentials that Parameter Store lacks natively.

solution.explanation: Configuration management for Lambda requires matching the access pattern and sensitivity level to the right storage mechanism. Environment variables are ideal for non-sensitive, per-environment configuration that doesn't change frequently — they incur no runtime latency because they're available as in-memory process variables, but they require a Lambda function update to change, making them inappropriate for dynamic feature flags. SSM Parameter Store provides externally managed configuration accessible via API, enabling real-time changes without redeployment — this is perfect for feature flags but requires caching to avoid both the API latency penalty and throttling limits (standard tier is 40 TPS). Secrets Manager is the appropriate choice for credentials requiring automatic rotation — it has built-in rotation Lambda blueprints for common databases and can rotate secrets on a schedule without manual intervention. A critical performance best practice for both Parameter Store and Secrets Manager is caching retrieved values in Lambda's global scope (outside the handler function) — warm invocations reuse the cached value, limiting API calls to once per execution environment lifetime or configured TTL.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Cache External Config in Global Scope
methodSignatures.description: Retrieve Parameter Store or Secrets Manager values ONCE in Lambda global scope (outside the handler), not inside the handler. Global scope code runs only during cold start (once per execution environment) — warm invocations skip it. This reduces API calls from N (one per invocation) to 1 (once per execution environment lifetime).

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Secrets Manager vs Parameter Store SecureString
methodSignatures.description: Both can store encrypted secrets. Key difference: Secrets Manager has automatic rotation, cross-account sharing, and costs $0.40/secret/month. Parameter Store SecureString is free (standard tier) but has no native auto-rotation. Choose Secrets Manager for anything that needs scheduled rotation (API keys, DB passwords). Use Parameter Store for configuration that needs encryption but not auto-rotation.

title: Lambda Execution Role: Granting Permissions to AWS Services
description: A new developer is writing a Lambda function that needs to write items to a DynamoDB table, publish messages to an SNS topic, and write logs to CloudWatch. When they deploy and test the function, it fails with 'Access Denied' when trying to write to DynamoDB. They are confused because they 'gave the function permissions' — but they created an IAM User for the function and stored the access keys as environment variables.
hints: Lambda functions are an AWS service and should use the same mechanism that EC2 instances use to access AWS services — without storing long-term credentials.
There is a specific type of IAM identity designed for AWS services to assume permissions — not for human users.
CloudWatch Logs access is needed for every Lambda function — there is a AWS managed policy that grants exactly this permission.

solution.explanation: Lambda functions are AWS service principals and follow the same IAM role-based access pattern as EC2 — the correct approach is an IAM Execution Role, not an IAM User. The execution role has a trust policy that allows the Lambda service to assume it, and the attached permission policies define exactly which AWS services and operations the function can perform. The AWS SDK running inside Lambda automatically retrieves temporary credentials from the execution role through the Lambda environment's internal credential provider, requiring zero credential configuration code. The IAM User + environment variables approach is fundamentally flawed: long-term access keys never expire, are visible in the Lambda console to anyone with access, and require manual rotation — all violations of AWS security best practices. The `AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole` managed policy is essential for every Lambda function because it grants the permissions to create and write to CloudWatch Logs; without it, Lambda executes but produces no observable logs, making debugging nearly impossible. On the exam, any question about how Lambda should access another AWS service should always have 'execution role' as the answer.

methodSignatures.description: Each Lambda function should have its own dedicated execution role with only the minimum permissions needed for that specific function. Sharing a single 'Lambda admin role' across all functions violates least privilege — if one function is compromised, the attacker gains access to all services that any Lambda function in the account can access.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Resource-Based Policy vs Execution Role
methodSignatures.description: Lambda has TWO types of policies: (1) Execution Role (identity-based): what services Lambda can CALL (DynamoDB, SNS, etc.). (2) Resource-based policy on Lambda itself: who can INVOKE Lambda (S3, API Gateway, other accounts). Both are required for different access patterns — execution role for outbound, resource-based policy for inbound invocation.

title: DynamoDB Table Design: Partition Key, Sort Key, and Access Patterns
description: You are designing a DynamoDB table for a social media application. The access patterns are: (1) get all posts by a specific user, (2) get a specific post by post ID, (3) get all posts by a user sorted by creation date (most recent first), and (4) get all comments for a specific post. You need to design the primary key structure to efficiently support all these access patterns without full table scans.
hints: DynamoDB's composite primary key (partition key + sort key) enables range queries within a partition — all items with the same partition key can be queried by sort key range.
A sort key can be queried with range operators (begins_with, between, >, <) — this enables 'get newest posts' without a full scan.
For access patterns that require querying on non-primary-key attributes, you need to create a Global Secondary Index (GSI).

solution.explanation: DynamoDB table design must begin with the access patterns — unlike relational databases where you normalize data and add queries later, DynamoDB requires you to know all required access patterns upfront and design the primary key structure to serve them efficiently. The composite primary key (partition key + sort key) is the primary tool for supporting range queries: all items sharing the same partition key can be queried and sorted by the sort key range, enabling operations like 'get all posts by user, sorted by date'. High cardinality partition keys are essential for even data distribution — using a low-cardinality attribute (like country code or status) as a partition key creates 'hot partitions' where a few partitions receive disproportionate read/write load, causing throttling. Single Table Design is an advanced pattern that stores multiple entity types in one table using key prefixes to prevent collisions, enabling efficient access to related entities with a single Query call. For the comment access pattern, either single-table design (comments as items with PK=postId) or a GSI on postId provides efficient access; creating a separate Comments table and doing a cross-table join is an anti-pattern in DynamoDB.

methodSignatures.description: Choose a partition key with high cardinality (many unique values) to distribute data evenly. Bad: status='active'/'inactive' (2 values, extreme hot partition). Good: userId, orderId, productId (millions of unique values, even distribution). Uneven distribution causes some partitions to be throttled while others are idle.

Query: uses primary key or GSI to locate items efficiently — reads only items in the target partition. Scan: reads EVERY item in the table and filters — extremely expensive for large tables. ALWAYS use Query over Scan. If your access pattern requires Scan, you need to redesign the table or add a GSI.

Sort key supports: =, <, >, <=, >=, between, begins_with. Using ISO8601 timestamps as sort keys enables begins_with('2024-01') to get all items from January 2024. Inverted timestamps (MAX_VALUE - timestamp) store newest items first, enabling newest-first queries without ScanIndexForward=false.

title: Slow DynamoDB Queries: Fixing Full Table Scans with GSI Design
description: An e-commerce application stores order data in DynamoDB with OrderId as the partition key. A new feature requires listing all orders with status='PENDING' sorted by createdAt date. The current implementation does a full table Scan with a FilterExpression on status. With 50 million orders in the table, this scan is taking 45 seconds, costing enormous amounts of read capacity, and causing throttling for other operations.
hints: DynamoDB Global Secondary Indexes let you define an alternate partition key and sort key for query access — similar to creating a secondary index in a relational database.
For the 'all orders by status sorted by date' pattern, status would be the partition key of the GSI and createdAt would be the sort key.
Consider whether a GSI with status as partition key would create a hot partition problem (PENDING might have millions of items).

solution.explanation: DynamoDB Scan with FilterExpression is the most expensive operation possible because FilterExpression is evaluated AFTER reading all items — you still consume Read Capacity Units for every item in the table even if 99% are filtered out. A Global Secondary Index solves this by creating an alternate index with a different partition key and sort key that matches the access pattern, enabling efficient Query operations instead of Scan. For the 'pending orders by date' pattern, a GSI with status as partition key and createdAt as sort key allows a Query on the GSI that reads only orders with the specified status, sorted by date. However, a naive status partition key creates a hot partition problem — if there are millions of pending orders, they all map to the same 'PENDING' partition, concentrating all read traffic to a single partition. The write sharding technique (appending a random shard number like 'PENDING#3') distributes items across multiple partitions at the cost of requiring parallel queries and client-side merging. LSIs must be created at table creation time, making them unsuitable for this scenario where the table already exists.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: FilterExpression Does NOT Reduce Consumed RCUs
methodSignatures.description: A FilterExpression on a Scan or Query is evaluated AFTER DynamoDB reads the items — you pay for ALL items read, not just the ones that pass the filter. To reduce cost, you must use the partition key in Query (reads only one partition) or add a GSI (reads only the index). FilterExpression is for post-read filtering of already-fetched items.

GSI Projection determines which attributes are copied to the index: KEYS_ONLY (cheapest storage), INCLUDE (specific attributes), ALL (all attributes, highest storage cost). If your query needs attributes not in the projection, DynamoDB must fetch the base table item (additional read). For read-heavy workloads, ALL projection avoids extra fetches at the cost of more storage.

title: DynamoDB Consistent Reads: When to Use Strong Consistency
description: A banking application uses DynamoDB to store account balances. A user transfers $500 from Account A to Account B. Immediately after the transfer, the application reads Account B's balance to display to the user. The displayed balance shows the old value (without the $500). The developer is confused because the write succeeded. They need to understand DynamoDB's consistency models and configure the read appropriately.
hints: DynamoDB replicates data across 3 Availability Zones. By default, reads may read from any replica, and updates may not have fully propagated yet.
There is a read option that guarantees you'll see the result of all successful writes that completed before the read.
Strongly consistent reads cost twice as many Read Capacity Units as eventually consistent reads.

solution.explanation: DynamoDB replicates all data across three Availability Zones for durability. By default (eventually consistent), a read can be served by any of the three replicas — if a write just completed on the leader node, it may not have propagated to the replicas yet, resulting in reading the pre-write value. This is by design and is perfectly acceptable for most use cases where the slight staleness window (typically milliseconds) doesn't affect correctness. Strongly consistent reads force the request to the leader node, which has the authoritative copy of all committed data, guaranteeing that the response reflects all writes that completed before the read. The two-times RCU cost reflects the additional resource usage of routing to the leader and waiting for confirmed consistency. A critical exam point is that GSIs do not support strongly consistent reads — if your application requires strong consistency for a non-primary-key access pattern, you must use the base table (primary key access) rather than a GSI. For the banking application, the correct pattern combines DynamoDB Transactions for the atomic debit/credit operation with strongly consistent reads for post-transaction balance verification.

methodSignatures.description: RCU (Read Capacity Unit): 1 RCU = 1 strongly consistent read OR 2 eventually consistent reads for items up to 4 KB. For a 6 KB item: strongly consistent = 2 RCUs (ceil(6/4)=2), eventually consistent = 1 RCU (ceil(6/4)/2=1). Transactional reads: 2 RCUs per 4 KB (2x the cost of strong consistency).

Global Secondary Indexes are updated asynchronously after the base table is written — there is always a brief propagation delay. Therefore, GSI reads are always eventually consistent; setting ConsistentRead=true on a GSI Query has no effect and does not raise an error. Design applications accordingly: if strong consistency is needed for an access pattern, use the base table primary key.

title: DynamoDB Streams + Lambda: Change Data Capture Pipeline
description: An e-commerce platform wants to build a real-time order fulfillment pipeline where every time an order status changes to 'SHIPPED' in DynamoDB, a notification Lambda is automatically triggered to send a shipping confirmation email. Additionally, the data analytics team needs a copy of all DynamoDB changes sent to Elasticsearch for search and analytics. You need to design a Change Data Capture (CDC) solution using DynamoDB Streams.
hints: DynamoDB Streams captures a time-ordered sequence of item-level changes and retains them for 24 hours.
Lambda can be configured as an event source for DynamoDB Streams — it receives batches of change records and can filter based on the content.
For fan-out to multiple consumers (Lambda email + Elasticsearch), there is a limitation on DynamoDB Streams readers per shard.

solution.explanation: DynamoDB Streams is a time-ordered log of all item-level changes that enables event-driven architectures and Change Data Capture (CDC) patterns. The stream view type determines how much data is captured per change: KEYS_ONLY is cheapest but only provides the changed item's key; NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES provides both the before and after state, enabling change detection logic like 'status changed from PROCESSING to SHIPPED'. Lambda event source mapping for DynamoDB Streams supports filter criteria that evaluate the event content before invoking Lambda — by filtering for `eventName=MODIFY AND newImage.status.S=SHIPPED`, you avoid invoking the Lambda function for unrelated changes, significantly reducing invocations and costs. A critical architectural constraint is the 2-reader-per-shard limit on DynamoDB Streams — for the fan-out requirement (email + Elasticsearch), the first Lambda consumes the stream and then publishes to SNS, which distributes to multiple downstream consumers. Alternatively, enabling DynamoDB Kinesis Streaming sends changes directly to a Kinesis Data Stream which has no reader limit and supports Enhanced Fan-Out for multiple parallel consumers.

methodSignatures.description: DynamoDB Streams only retains records for 24 hours. If your Lambda consumer is down or throttled for more than 24 hours, those change events are permanently lost. For critical CDC pipelines, enable DynamoDB Kinesis Streaming (routes to Kinesis Data Streams) which supports configurable retention up to 365 days.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Lambda Filter Criteria for Streams
methodSignatures.description: Lambda event source mapping supports filter criteria using JSON path patterns. Example to filter only SHIPPED orders: {"eventName": ["MODIFY"], "dynamodb": {"NewImage": {"status": {"S": ["SHIPPED"]}}}}. Filtering happens before Lambda is invoked — filtered-out records are not billed as Lambda invocations.

title: DynamoDB TTL: Automatically Expiring Session Data
description: A web application stores user session data in DynamoDB. Sessions should automatically expire after 24 hours of creation. Currently, a scheduled Lambda function runs every hour to scan the table and delete expired sessions — this is expensive (full table scan on a large table) and the Lambda costs are significant. The team wants a more efficient and cost-effective solution.
hints: DynamoDB has a built-in feature that automatically deletes items based on a timestamp attribute — no external Lambda or scan required.
The TTL attribute must contain a Unix epoch timestamp (seconds since January 1, 1970) that represents when the item should expire.
TTL deletion is not instantaneous — there is a window during which expired items may still be visible to reads.

solution.explanation: DynamoDB TTL is a zero-cost automatic cleanup mechanism that eliminates the need for external Lambda scanning and deletion jobs. By adding a numeric timestamp attribute to each item and enabling TTL on the table for that attribute, DynamoDB's background process monitors and deletes expired items without consuming any write capacity. The trade-off is that deletion is asynchronous — DynamoDB guarantees deletion within 48 hours of expiry, but typically processes within minutes to a few hours. This means your application may still query and receive expired items if you don't filter them; adding a `FilterExpression` to exclude items past their TTL ensures stale data is not displayed. The TTL attribute must be a Number type containing Unix epoch seconds (not milliseconds — using milliseconds is a common mistake that results in items being deleted immediately or items never expiring). TTL deletions do appear in DynamoDB Streams as REMOVE events, which enables downstream CDC pipelines to also clean up related data in other systems (like caches or search indexes).

methodSignatures.description: DynamoDB TTL requires epoch time in SECONDS. JavaScript's Date.now() returns milliseconds — divide by 1000. Python's time.time() returns seconds (correct). If you accidentally use milliseconds, your TTL value will be ~1000 years in the future and items will never expire. Always verify your TTL attribute contains a reasonable near-future timestamp.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: TTL Does Not Consume WCU
methodSignatures.description: DynamoDB TTL deletions are free — they do NOT consume Write Capacity Units from your table's provisioned or on-demand capacity. This makes TTL far more cost-effective than manual deletion via a scan + batch delete (which would consume both Read Capacity Units for scanning and Write Capacity Units for deleting).

title: Optimistic Locking with DynamoDB Condition Expressions
description: A travel booking application stores seat availability in DynamoDB. Multiple users can simultaneously view and attempt to book the last available seat on a flight. Without proper concurrency control, two users could both book the same seat (overselling). The application currently reads the current count, decrements it, and writes the new value — a classic read-modify-write race condition. You need to implement optimistic locking to prevent overselling.
hints: DynamoDB Condition Expressions allow you to make a write operation conditional — the write only succeeds if the condition evaluates to true at the time of the write.
In optimistic locking, you read a value, compute a new value, then write with a condition that the value hasn't changed since you read it — if it has, you retry.
DynamoDB also supports atomic increment/decrement operations that don't require read-modify-write cycles at all.

solution.explanation: Condition Expressions in DynamoDB enable optimistic concurrency control by making write operations conditional on the current state of the item at the time of the write — the condition is evaluated atomically on the server side, eliminating the race condition window. In the seat booking scenario, the Condition Expression `seatCount = :expectedCount` ensures that if another user has already modified the count since we read it, our write fails rather than blindly overwriting their change. The application catches `ConditionalCheckFailedException`, re-reads the current state, and either retries the booking or informs the user the seat is no longer available. The atomic counter approach using `ADD seatCount :decrement` with a condition `seatCount > 0` is even more elegant for this specific use case — it eliminates the read step entirely by performing an atomic decrement on the server, which prevents negative counts and race conditions simultaneously. Condition Expressions are the DynamoDB equivalent of SQL's WHERE clause in UPDATE statements and are evaluated without consuming additional capacity units.

methodSignatures.description: Use ConditionExpression: 'attribute_not_exists(PK)' to ensure a PutItem only succeeds if the item doesn't already exist. This is critical for idempotent operations: if a Lambda retries a failed PutItem and the first attempt actually succeeded, the retry will get ConditionalCheckFailedException, telling you the item was already created — no duplicate write.

When a Condition Expression fails, DynamoDB can return the current item values that caused the failure (ReturnValuesOnConditionCheckFailure=ALL_OLD). This saves a round-trip read after a failed condition check — you already know the current state that caused the failure and can decide to retry or return an error without an additional GetItem call.

title: DynamoDB Capacity Modes: On-Demand vs Provisioned with Auto Scaling
description: A startup is launching a new mobile game. During beta testing, traffic is highly unpredictable — could be 10 requests/second or 10,000 requests/second at any moment. In six months they expect to have a stable, predictable load of about 5,000 reads and 1,000 writes per second. They need to choose between DynamoDB's capacity modes for both phases of growth.
hints: On-Demand mode charges per request, scales automatically with no capacity planning — ideal for unpredictable workloads.
Provisioned mode charges per provisioned capacity unit per hour — cheaper for steady, predictable loads but requires you to specify the throughput.
DynamoDB Auto Scaling for Provisioned mode adjusts capacity automatically based on CloudWatch metrics, bridging the gap between the two modes.

solution.explanation: DynamoDB's two capacity modes optimize for different cost profiles. On-Demand mode eliminates capacity planning by charging per request and scaling automatically — this is ideal for beta phase where traffic is unpredictable, as there is no risk of throttling and no capacity management overhead. However, On-Demand is significantly more expensive per request at high, consistent throughput. Once traffic patterns stabilize, switching to Provisioned mode with properly sized capacity and Auto Scaling dramatically reduces costs — Provisioned charges per capacity unit per hour regardless of actual usage, which means it rewards consistent, predictable workloads where most provisioned capacity is utilized. Auto Scaling bridges the gap by automatically adjusting provisioned capacity based on utilization targets, but it has a scaling reaction lag (typically minutes) and is not suitable for instantaneous traffic spikes — for those, DynamoDB provides a burst capacity buffer from unused capacity accumulated over the past 5 minutes. On the exam, 'unpredictable or new workload' maps to On-Demand, while 'predictable steady-state workload' maps to Provisioned mode.

methodSignatures.description: You can switch a DynamoDB table between On-Demand and Provisioned modes, but only ONCE per 24 hours. Plan capacity mode changes carefully — you cannot switch back immediately if you make a mistake. When switching from On-Demand to Provisioned, start with a capacity estimate based on CloudWatch metrics from your On-Demand usage.

DynamoDB retains unused provisioned capacity as 'burst capacity' for up to 5 minutes. If your table is normally using 500 out of 1,000 provisioned WCUs, it accumulates 500 WCU/sec × 300 seconds = 150,000 burst WCUs. Brief spikes consume this burst capacity before throttling occurs. Burst capacity helps absorb short traffic spikes but is not a substitute for proper capacity planning.

title: DynamoDB Transactions: Atomic Multi-Item Operations
description: A marketplace application needs to implement a purchase flow that must atomically: (1) decrement the item's available inventory by 1, (2) create an order record, and (3) deduct the purchase amount from the user's account balance. If any one of these operations fails (insufficient inventory, insufficient balance, order creation error), ALL operations must be rolled back. Additionally, before writing, you must verify that the item is still available and the user has sufficient balance.
hints: DynamoDB provides a TransactWriteItems API that makes up to 100 items' writes atomic across up to 10 different tables.
The transaction can include condition checks that verify preconditions (inventory > 0, balance >= amount) before any writes are committed.
Transactional operations cost 2x the normal capacity units.

solution.explanation: DynamoDB Transactions provide ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) guarantees for multi-item operations that would otherwise require complex application-level compensation logic. The `TransactWriteItems` API accepts up to 100 actions (Put, Update, Delete, ConditionCheck) across up to 10 tables and executes them as a single atomic unit — if any action's condition fails or any write fails, DynamoDB automatically rolls back all changes. The `ConditionCheck` action is particularly useful: it allows you to verify a precondition (like inventory > 0) without actually writing to that item, while still being part of the all-or-nothing transaction. When a transaction fails, the `TransactionCanceledException` includes a `CancellationReasons` array that identifies which specific item's condition failed, enabling precise error handling and user feedback. The 2x capacity cost reflects the additional work DynamoDB performs for conflict detection and rollback coordination. For high-throughput scenarios, consider whether all three operations truly need to be transactional, as the 2x cost can be significant at scale.

methodSignatures.description: TransactWriteItems supports a ClientRequestToken for idempotency — if the same token is reused within 10 minutes, DynamoDB returns the same result without reprocessing. This is critical for safely retrying transactions after network failures: you don't know if the first attempt succeeded, so using the same idempotency token prevents double-charging or double-booking on retry.

TransactionCanceledException means the transaction was cancelled because a condition check failed (expected, handle in application logic). TransactionConflictException means two concurrent transactions tried to modify the same items simultaneously — DynamoDB detected the conflict and rejected one (retry with exponential backoff). These are distinct errors requiring different handling.

title: REST API vs HTTP API vs WebSocket API: Choosing the Right Type
description: A developer needs to build three different APIs: (1) a customer-facing CRUD API for a web app with standard request/response patterns, custom authorizers, and per-client usage tracking, (2) a real-time chat feature where the server needs to push messages to connected clients without the client polling, and (3) a high-throughput mobile backend that needs the lowest possible latency and cost, using JWT authentication only. They need to choose the right API Gateway type for each.
hints: One API type supports bidirectional persistent connections where the server can initiate message delivery to clients — ideal for real-time features.
The REST API type has the most features (WAF, usage plans, caching, API keys) but is more expensive than the newer HTTP API type.
HTTP API is up to 70% cheaper than REST API and supports OIDC/JWT authorization natively but lacks usage plans, API keys, and request/response transformation.

solution.explanation: API Gateway offers three distinct types optimized for different communication patterns. REST API is the most feature-rich option supporting usage plans, API keys, per-method throttling, request/response transformation, edge optimization through CloudFront, and AWS WAF integration — making it the appropriate choice for APIs requiring sophisticated traffic management and security controls. HTTP API is a streamlined, modern alternative that provides significantly lower cost (up to 70% cheaper) and lower latency by eliminating features that many applications don't need; it supports JWT/OIDC natively but lacks usage plans, API keys, and transformation capabilities. WebSocket API solves a fundamentally different problem: persistent bidirectional connections where the server can proactively push data to clients — this is essential for real-time features like chat, live dashboards, and collaborative editing where polling would be inefficient. The exam frequently tests knowing which API Gateway type supports which features — the most common trap is using REST API when HTTP API is sufficient (wasting 70% more on cost) or not knowing that API keys and usage plans are REST-API-exclusive features.

methodSignatures.description: REST API Gateway supports response caching with configurable TTL (0-3600 seconds). Cached responses are returned for identical requests without invoking Lambda, reducing cost and latency. Cache invalidation can be triggered by callers with the Cache-Control: max-age=0 header (if the cache is configured to honor this). HTTP API does NOT support caching.

WebSocket API maintains connection state externally (Lambda is stateless). Use DynamoDB to store active connectionIds. When sending messages to clients, Lambda must call the API Gateway Management API (POST to @connections/{connectionId}). Handle GoneException when connectionId is no longer valid (client disconnected).

title: API Gateway Authorization: Lambda Authorizer vs Cognito vs IAM
description: A company is designing authorization for three different API use cases: (1) a public API used by third-party partners who authenticate with custom OAuth tokens from a non-AWS identity provider, (2) a mobile app where users log in with email/password and the app needs JWT tokens that API Gateway validates automatically, and (3) an internal microservice API that should only be called by other AWS services or IAM roles within the same organization.
hints: For custom token validation logic (especially from non-AWS identity providers), API Gateway can invoke a Lambda function to perform the validation.
Cognito User Pool Authorizer natively validates JWTs issued by AWS Cognito without requiring custom Lambda code.
IAM authorization uses SigV4 signing — the caller signs the request with their AWS credentials, and API Gateway validates the signature.

solution.explanation: API Gateway supports three built-in authorization mechanisms each solving a different authentication scenario. Lambda Authorizers are the most flexible: a Lambda function receives the request's authorization token (or all request attributes for request-type authorizers), performs any custom validation logic (verify against external IdP, database lookup, custom business rules), and returns an IAM Allow/Deny policy — API Gateway caches this result to avoid repeated Lambda invocations for the same token. Cognito User Pool Authorizers handle the most common consumer use case: API Gateway natively validates JWTs issued by Cognito without requiring custom code, checking the token signature, expiry, and claims automatically. IAM Authorization uses AWS SigV4 request signing, which is appropriate for service-to-service calls where the caller is an AWS principal — no custom code is needed, but the caller must have AWS credentials to sign requests. A common confusion on the exam is between Cognito User Pools (authentication service, issues JWTs, for API Gateway authorization) and Cognito Identity Pools (exchanges any federated token for temporary AWS credentials, for accessing AWS services directly).

methodSignatures.description: A Lambda Authorizer must return a valid IAM policy document with Principal, Effect, Action (execute-api:Invoke), and Resource (API ARN). You can also return a context object with custom key-value pairs that are forwarded to the backend Lambda. Missing the correct ARN format for the Resource field is a common source of authorization failures.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Cognito User Pool vs Identity Pool
methodSignatures.description: User Pool = manages user directory, handles signup/login, issues JWTs (used for API Gateway authorization). Identity Pool = exchanges any identity (User Pool JWT, Google, Facebook, custom) for temporary AWS credentials via STS — lets mobile apps call AWS services directly. For API authorization: User Pool. For direct AWS service access from mobile: Identity Pool.

title: API Gateway Throttling and Usage Plans: Preventing API Abuse
description: A company exposes a public REST API to paying customers. Free tier customers should be limited to 100 requests/minute with a burst of 200; premium customers get 1,000 requests/minute with a burst of 2,000. Regardless of tier, no single API method should receive more than 500 requests/second from all customers combined. Additionally, a monitoring dashboard needs to track how much each customer is consuming.
hints: API Keys identify individual API consumers — when combined with Usage Plans, they control per-consumer rate limits.
API Gateway has account-level, stage-level, and method-level throttling — the most restrictive limit at each level applies.
Usage Plans define the rate and quota limits applied to API keys, enabling different tiers for different customer types.

solution.explanation: API Gateway throttling operates at three levels: account-level (hard floor for the entire account), stage-level (applies to all methods in a deployment stage collectively), and method-level (per-operation overrides). Usage Plans and API Keys work together for per-customer rate limiting: API Keys identify individual consumers, Usage Plans define the rate and burst limits for a tier, and API Keys are associated with specific Usage Plans — API Gateway enforces these limits per key. Stage-level throttling addresses the requirement of limiting total load on any single API method across all customers combined, while method-level throttling allows different limits for computationally expensive operations versus simple ones. An important distinction: API Keys are NOT an authentication mechanism — they identify clients for billing and rate limiting purposes, but authentication (who are you?) must be handled separately through Cognito, Lambda Authorizers, or IAM. When throttled, API Gateway immediately returns 429 Too Many Requests; the caller is responsible for implementing retry with exponential backoff.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: API Keys Are Not Authentication
methodSignatures.description: API Keys identify clients for usage tracking and throttling — they are NOT a security/authentication mechanism. API Key values can be shared or stolen like passwords. For actual security, use API Keys in COMBINATION with Cognito, Lambda Authorizer, or IAM authorization. Never use API Keys alone for sensitive APIs.

API Gateway returns 429 Too Many Requests when a client exceeds throttling limits. 429 is also the error from Lambda Throttling (when Lambda's concurrency limit is hit). When debugging 429 errors, check both API Gateway throttling metrics (Count metric + 4XXError) and Lambda ConcurrentExecutions + Throttles metrics to identify which layer is throttling.

title: API Gateway Caching: Reducing Lambda Invocations and Latency
description: A REST API backed by Lambda serves product catalog data that changes at most once per hour. The API is receiving 50,000 requests per minute with 99% of requests being for the same 100 popular products. Without caching, each request invokes a Lambda function that queries DynamoDB — resulting in high Lambda costs, DynamoDB read costs, and unnecessary latency. The team wants to implement API Gateway caching to reduce costs and improve response times.
hints: API Gateway caching is configured at the stage level and caches responses based on the request's path, query string, and optionally headers.
The cache TTL determines how long a response is kept before API Gateway fetches a fresh response from the backend.
Clients can bypass the cache with a specific request header if the API is configured to honor cache-control headers.

solution.explanation: API Gateway response caching stores Lambda/backend responses in an in-memory cache and serves subsequent identical requests directly from cache without invoking the backend. For a product catalog with 50,000 requests/minute where 99% request the same 100 products, a 1-hour TTL cache would reduce Lambda invocations from 50,000/minute to approximately 100 invocations/hour (one cache population per product per hour), achieving ~99.97% cost reduction in Lambda and DynamoDB costs. The cache key determines what constitutes a 'unique' request — by default it's the HTTP method and path, but you can include query string parameters and headers. Including the Authorization header in the cache key would create a separate cache entry per user, eliminating the benefit for a shared product catalog (each user would need their own cached response). Cache invalidation can be forced by clients using `Cache-Control: max-age=0`, but this should require authorization to prevent cache flooding attacks. API Gateway caching is exclusive to REST API — HTTP API does not support caching.

methodSignatures.description: Choose cache size based on expected number of unique cached responses × average response size. For 100 products × 10 KB/response = 1 MB of unique data — 0.5 GB cache would hold all unique responses with room to spare. Oversizing wastes hourly cost; undersizing causes frequent cache evictions. Monitor CacheHitCount and CacheMissCount metrics to validate cache efficiency.

While cache is enabled at stage level, individual methods can override the TTL or disable caching entirely. For example, a GET /user/profile endpoint might need TTL=0 (no cache) because responses are user-specific, while GET /catalog can use TTL=3600. Configure per-method overrides in the Stage Editor under each resource/method.

title: CORS Configuration in API Gateway for Browser-Based Applications
description: A single-page React application hosted at `https://app.example.com` calls a REST API deployed at `https://api.example.com`. The browser console shows: 'Access to fetch at https://api.example.com/data from origin https://app.example.com has been blocked by CORS policy'. The developer has confirmed the API itself works correctly when called from Postman. They need to understand CORS and fix the API Gateway configuration.
hints: CORS is enforced by browsers (not servers) — Postman doesn't send preflight requests, which is why it works. Browsers send an OPTIONS preflight before non-simple requests.
The API Gateway must respond to OPTIONS requests with the correct CORS headers before the browser allows the actual request.
For Lambda proxy integration, the CORS headers must also be included in the Lambda function's response, not just in API Gateway's OPTIONS response.

solution.explanation: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security policy that prevents web pages from making requests to a different domain than the one that served the page — this prevents malicious scripts from silently making API calls on behalf of users. Browsers enforce CORS; tools like Postman are not browsers and make requests directly without the CORS restriction, which is why the same API call works in Postman but fails in the browser. For non-simple HTTP requests, browsers send an OPTIONS preflight request to check if the server allows the actual request's origin, method, and headers; the server must respond with the appropriate `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers. In API Gateway, enabling CORS creates an OPTIONS route/method with a mock response returning the required headers. The critical mistake in Lambda proxy integration is forgetting that Lambda must also include CORS headers in every response (not just the OPTIONS handler) — the browser checks CORS headers on the actual response, not just the preflight. HTTP API handles this more cleanly by allowing CORS configuration at the API level, automatically injecting CORS headers without requiring Lambda code changes.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Credentials and CORS Origin Wildcard
methodSignatures.description: If your API requires credentials (cookies, HTTP authentication, or the Authorization header), you CANNOT use * as the Access-Control-Allow-Origin value — you must specify the exact origin. Also set Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true in the response. Using * with credentials causes browsers to reject the response even if the preflight succeeded.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Lambda Proxy Must Return CORS Headers
methodSignatures.description: When using Lambda proxy integration, API Gateway passes Lambda's response directly to the browser. Lambda must explicitly include Access-Control-Allow-Origin in every response object. A common bug: OPTIONS preflight works (API Gateway handles it), but actual GET/POST requests fail because Lambda forgot to include the CORS header in its response.

title: Decoupling a Monolith: Order Service Overwhelming Fulfillment with SQS and DLQ
description: An e-commerce platform's order service is directly calling the fulfillment service via synchronous HTTP. During flash sales, the order service creates 5,000 orders/minute while the fulfillment service can only process 500 orders/minute. Orders are being dropped and customers are not receiving their confirmation emails. The system needs to be decoupled so orders are not lost during peak periods, with a strategy for handling orders that ultimately fail processing after multiple retries.
hints: SQS acts as a buffer between producers and consumers — messages persist until a consumer successfully processes them, absorbing traffic spikes.
A Dead Letter Queue receives messages that have failed processing more than a configurable number of times (maxReceiveCount).
The visibility timeout must be longer than the maximum expected processing time — otherwise, a message being processed will become visible again and be picked up by another consumer.

solution.explanation: SQS solves the producer-consumer speed mismatch by acting as a durable, elastic buffer. When the order service sends to SQS instead of calling fulfillment directly, orders are never dropped — they persist in the queue (up to 14 days) until the fulfillment service processes them at its own rate. The asynchronous model means the order service can return an immediate acknowledgment to the customer while the fulfillment pipeline works through the backlog. Visibility timeout is the mechanism that prevents duplicate processing: when a consumer retrieves a message, it becomes 'invisible' for the timeout duration, preventing other consumers from processing the same message while the first is working on it. If processing completes successfully, the consumer deletes the message; if it fails or crashes, the message reappears after the timeout for another attempt. The Dead Letter Queue captures messages that repeatedly fail processing (after `maxReceiveCount` receive attempts), isolating problem messages from the main queue so they don't block other orders while still being preserved for investigation.

methodSignatures.description: Set visibility timeout to at least 6x the Lambda/consumer timeout if using Lambda as the consumer. If processing takes up to 5 minutes, set visibility timeout to 30 minutes. Alternatively, extend the visibility timeout programmatically mid-processing if you detect it will take longer than expected. Too-short timeout is the #1 cause of SQS message duplication.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: DLQ for SQS vs Lambda Async DLQ
methodSignatures.description: SQS DLQ (redrive policy): messages go to DLQ after maxReceiveCount failures — triggered by consumer NOT deleting the message. Lambda async DLQ: events go to DLQ when Lambda fails processing after retries — different mechanism. When Lambda uses SQS as an event source, use the SQS DLQ (on the SQS queue), not the Lambda destination, for failed event handling.

title: Standard Queue vs FIFO Queue: Ordering, Throughput, and Deduplication
description: A development team is debating which SQS queue type to use for two different workloads: (1) a financial transaction processing system where each transaction must be processed exactly once and in the exact order it was submitted (a deposit followed by a withdrawal must be processed in that order), and (2) a thumbnail generation system where millions of images need to be processed as fast as possible and order doesn't matter.
hints: Standard queues offer 'at-least-once' delivery (messages may be delivered more than once) and 'best-effort ordering' (approximate ordering only).
FIFO queues guarantee exactly-once processing and strict first-in-first-out ordering, but are limited in throughput.
FIFO queues require a MessageGroupId — messages with the same group ID are processed in FIFO order, while different groups can be processed in parallel.

solution.explanation: Standard SQS queues prioritize throughput over ordering and deduplication — they provide 'at-least-once' delivery (the same message might be delivered multiple times) and 'best-effort' ordering (messages are usually delivered in order but not guaranteed). This makes them ideal for high-volume workloads like image processing where the consumer logic is idempotent and order is irrelevant. FIFO queues guarantee strict first-in-first-out ordering within a MessageGroup and exactly-once processing through deduplication, but are limited to 300 transactions per second (or 3,000 with batching). The `MessageGroupId` is a partition key within the FIFO queue — all messages sharing the same group ID are processed in order, while different group IDs are processed in parallel, enabling higher aggregate throughput while preserving per-entity ordering. For financial transactions at 500 TPS, the throughput can be achieved through batching or by using `userId` as `MessageGroupId`, parallelizing across many user accounts while maintaining per-user transaction ordering.

methodSignatures.description: FIFO queue deduplication works within a 5-minute window. If you send a message with the same MessageDeduplicationId twice within 5 minutes, the second is discarded. After 5 minutes, you can resend with the same ID and it will be treated as a new message. This protects against retry storms but not long-term duplicate prevention.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Idempotent Consumers for Standard Queues
methodSignatures.description: Standard queue at-least-once delivery means your consumer MUST be idempotent — processing the same message twice should not cause data corruption. Common pattern: use DynamoDB conditional writes with the SQS message ID as the idempotency key. If the insert fails (ConditionalCheckFailed), the message was already processed — skip and delete from queue.

title: SQS Visibility Timeout: Diagnosing Double Message Processing
description: A developer is experiencing strange behavior in a payment processing application: some payments are being charged to customers twice. Investigation reveals the payment processor reads an order from SQS, calls the payment API (which takes 45 seconds), and then deletes the message. The SQS queue's visibility timeout is set to 30 seconds. The developer needs to diagnose why messages are being processed twice and understand the correct configuration.
hints: When a consumer reads a message, it becomes 'invisible' for the visibility timeout duration. After the timeout expires, the message becomes visible again even if the consumer hasn't deleted it yet.
The payment processing takes 45 seconds but the visibility timeout is only 30 seconds — what happens at second 30?
SQS provides an API to extend the visibility timeout of a message that is currently being processed.

solution.explanation: The double payment is caused by a visibility timeout configured shorter than the actual processing time. When a consumer reads a message from SQS, the message is hidden from other consumers for the visibility timeout period — this is intentional to prevent duplicate processing while the first consumer is working. However, if the consumer doesn't delete the message before the timeout expires, SQS assumes the processing failed (consumer crashed, or took too long) and makes the message visible again, allowing another consumer to pick it up. In this case, Consumer A is still alive and processing, but Consumer B has also started processing the same message — both complete successfully and charge the customer twice. The fix is to either increase the visibility timeout to be longer than the maximum expected processing time, or to programmatically extend the visibility timeout during long-running processing using the `ChangeMessageVisibility` API. For financial operations, implementing idempotency at the payment API level (using a unique idempotency key per order) provides a critical safety net even if visibility timeout misconfiguration occurs.

methodSignatures.description: The SQS ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage CloudWatch metric indicates if messages are spending too long in the queue. If this metric grows, consumers are too slow or frequently failing. Monitor SQS NumberOfMessagesSent vs NumberOfMessagesDeleted to understand queue depth trends and right-size both visibility timeout and consumer throughput.

For unpredictably long processing jobs, implement a heartbeat: a background thread calls ChangeMessageVisibility every (timeout/2) seconds to extend the timeout. If the processing completes, delete the message. If the process crashes, the heartbeat stops, the timeout eventually expires, and the message returns to the queue for retry. This handles both slow and crashed consumers.

title: Fan-Out Pattern: SNS + SQS for One-to-Many Event Distribution
description: An e-commerce platform processes order events. When a new order is placed, multiple downstream services must be notified: the inventory service must reserve stock, the shipping service must create a shipping label, the notification service must send a confirmation email, and the analytics service must record the event. All four services must receive every order event, must process at their own pace, and must not lose events if temporarily down.
hints: If the Order Service sends directly to 4 SQS queues, it must know about all downstream services — tight coupling. Adding a 5th service requires changing the Order Service.
SNS allows publishers and subscribers to be decoupled — the publisher sends to one topic, and any number of subscribers receive a copy.
SQS queues subscribed to an SNS topic receive a copy of every message — messages persist in the queue until the downstream service processes them.

solution.explanation: The SNS + SQS fan-out pattern is the fundamental AWS design for one-to-many event distribution. SNS (Simple Notification Service) provides the decoupling hub — publishers send to a topic without knowing who subscribes, and any service can subscribe or unsubscribe without affecting the publisher. By using SQS queues as SNS subscribers rather than direct Lambda/HTTP endpoints, each downstream service gets a durable, independently managed buffer: if the Shipping service is down for 2 hours, the messages accumulate in its SQS queue and are processed when it recovers, without affecting Inventory or Analytics. The alternative of having the Order Service write directly to all four queues creates tight coupling — the Order Service must know about and maintain connections to all downstream services, and adding a new service requires deploying an Order Service change. With SNS fan-out, the Order Service only knows the topic ARN; adding a 5th service is a pure infrastructure change (subscribe new SQS to topic). SNS FIFO topics can fan-out to SQS FIFO queues when strict ordering must be preserved across fan-out destinations.

methodSignatures.description: If SNS cannot deliver a message to a subscriber (SQS queue full, HTTP endpoint down), SNS retries with exponential backoff. For HTTP endpoints: retries over 23 days. For SQS: if queue's maximum message size is exceeded or queue doesn't exist, delivery fails — configure SNS DLQ (on the SNS subscription, not the SQS queue) to capture failed deliveries.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: SNS + S3 Event Notification Alternative
methodSignatures.description: For S3 events with fan-out requirements, use S3 → SNS → (SQS, Lambda, Email) instead of S3 → Lambda → multiple targets. S3 directly supports SNS as an event notification target, and SNS handles the fan-out. This avoids having a 'dispatcher Lambda' that just routes events to other services.

title: SNS Message Filtering: Routing Subsets of Messages to Subscribers
description: An e-commerce platform publishes all order events to one SNS topic. The topic has three SQS queue subscribers: a fraud detection queue (only needs orders over $500), a priority fulfillment queue (only needs orders marked as 'URGENT' priority), and a general fulfillment queue (needs all other orders that are not URGENT). Without filtering, all three queues receive every order event, wasting processing resources and causing the fraud detection service to evaluate low-value orders unnecessarily.
hints: SNS allows you to attach a filter policy to each subscription, not to the topic itself — each subscriber can have different filtering criteria.
Message attributes must be added to the SNS message by the publisher for filter policies to evaluate them.
SNS can filter based on message attributes (keys and values) or on specific fields within a JSON message body (newer feature).

solution.explanation: SNS message filtering allows each subscription to define criteria for which messages it wants to receive, enabling a single SNS topic to efficiently route different message types to different subscribers without changing the publisher. Filter policies are applied at the subscription level, meaning the same topic can have subscriptions with completely different filter criteria. The publisher includes message attributes (or structured JSON body fields) that SNS evaluates against each subscriber's filter policy before deciding whether to deliver. This pattern eliminates the need for a routing Lambda that reads all messages and re-routes them — the routing is done by SNS natively with zero processing cost. A common misconception is that messages failing a filter go to a DLQ — they don't; they are simply not delivered to that subscriber. Filter policies support both attribute-based filtering (using message attributes added by the publisher) and body-based filtering (filtering on fields in a structured JSON message body, enabled via `FilterPolicyScope=MessageBody`).

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Filter Policy AND vs OR Logic
methodSignatures.description: In an SNS filter policy: different attribute conditions (separate keys) are evaluated with AND logic (all must match). Multiple values within one attribute's condition array are evaluated with OR logic (any value matches). Example: {"priority": ["URGENT", "HIGH"], "amount": [{"numeric": [">", 100]}]} means (priority = URGENT OR HIGH) AND (amount > 100).

A message that doesn't match any subscription's filter policy is simply not delivered to that subscription — it is NOT sent to a DLQ or stored anywhere. This is fine for optional routing scenarios. If a message MUST be delivered somewhere, ensure at least one subscription has no filter policy (or a catch-all policy) to receive all messages.

title: SQS Long Polling vs Short Polling: Cost and Latency Tradeoffs
description: A developer has a consumer application that polls an SQS queue for new messages. The application polls every second but messages only arrive about once per minute on average. AWS bills are showing unexpectedly high SQS API call costs, and the team notices that 95% of the poll requests return empty responses (no messages). They need to understand how to optimize polling to reduce costs without significantly increasing message processing latency.
hints: Short polling queries only a subset of SQS servers and returns immediately (even if no messages exist). Long polling waits for the specified duration before returning if no messages are immediately available.
Long polling reduces empty responses and therefore API call costs by waiting for messages to arrive rather than immediately returning empty.
Long polling can be configured on the queue itself or per-receive-message API call.

solution.explanation: Short polling queries a subset of SQS distributed servers and returns immediately, even if no messages are available — this results in many empty responses, each costing the same as a successful poll. Long polling instructs SQS to query all servers and wait up to a specified duration (maximum 20 seconds) for messages to arrive before returning. If a message arrives during the wait period, it's returned immediately without waiting the full duration — so long polling doesn't add latency for messages that are available. The cost benefit is significant: in a scenario where messages arrive once per minute, 20-second long polling reduces API calls from 60/minute to approximately 3/minute (one call waits 20 seconds, immediately returns when message arrives; then next call starts). Long polling also improves reliability because it queries all SQS servers rather than a subset, reducing the chance of missing messages that exist on servers not queried during short polling. AWS Lambda's SQS event source mapping uses long polling automatically, which is one reason it's more efficient than writing custom polling code.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Long Polling with Lambda Event Source
methodSignatures.description: When Lambda uses SQS as an event source (event source mapping), Lambda's internal poller automatically uses long polling (20 seconds) — you don't need to configure anything. Lambda manages the polling infrastructure, scales the number of pollers based on queue depth, and batches messages efficiently. This is one of the managed advantages of Lambda + SQS over self-managed EC2 + SQS.

If you implement long polling in application code, ensure your HTTP client has a timeout longer than 20 seconds (add a buffer, e.g., 25 seconds). SQS long polling can hold the connection for up to 20 seconds — a client with a 15-second timeout will close the connection early and retry, defeating the purpose of long polling.

title: RDS Multi-AZ vs Read Replicas: High Availability vs Read Scaling
description: A startup's CTO asks you to explain two commonly confused RDS features before they deploy a production database: Multi-AZ deployments and Read Replicas. The application currently experiences both database failures causing downtime AND slow read performance due to complex analytics queries running alongside the OLTP workload. They want to understand which feature solves which problem and whether they can use both simultaneously.
hints: Multi-AZ is about high availability — it keeps a standby copy in sync for automatic failover, but the standby cannot serve read traffic.
Read Replicas are about performance — they create asynchronous copies that can serve read traffic, reducing load on the primary.
Multi-AZ failover is automatic (RDS manages it); Read Replica promotion is a manual operation.

solution.explanation: Multi-AZ and Read Replicas solve different problems and are frequently confused. Multi-AZ maintains a synchronous hot standby in a different AZ — every write to the primary is committed to the standby before acknowledging success, ensuring zero data loss. When the primary fails, RDS automatically updates the CNAME record to point to the standby, completing failover in 60-120 seconds without any manual intervention. Critically, the Multi-AZ standby is NOT accessible for reads — it exists solely as a failover target. Read Replicas are asynchronously maintained copies that CAN serve read traffic, allowing you to route analytics queries and reporting to a separate instance so they don't compete with OLTP operations on the primary. The asynchronous nature means Read Replicas may have a replication lag and should not be used for reads that require guaranteed up-to-date data. Using both Multi-AZ AND Read Replicas together is a best practice for production databases: Multi-AZ protects against primary failure while Read Replicas handle read scalability and analytics offloading simultaneously.

methodSignatures.description: Monitor ReadReplicaLag CloudWatch metric to detect replication lag on Read Replicas. High lag (> a few seconds) means reads from the replica may return significantly stale data. Causes include: heavy write load on primary exceeding replica apply speed, network issues, or replica instance being too small. Never route strongly-consistent-required reads to a Read Replica.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Multi-AZ Failover and Connection Strings
methodSignatures.description: RDS Multi-AZ failover changes which instance the DNS endpoint resolves to. Applications must use the RDS endpoint hostname (not IP address) and configure short DNS TTL and connection retry logic. After failover, existing TCP connections are dropped — implement connection retry/reconnect logic in your application or use RDS Proxy (which handles failover transparently to the application).

title: RDS Performance Bottleneck: Read Replicas, ElastiCache, and Query Optimization
description: A media website's MySQL RDS instance is becoming a bottleneck. CPU is at 80%, read latency is high, and the instance is approaching its connection limit (500 connections, 480 currently). The workload is 90% reads (article views, search results) and 10% writes (content updates). The team needs to identify multiple complementary strategies to address the performance issues.
hints: For frequently read, rarely changed data (like popular articles), a cache can serve requests without hitting the database at all.
Read Replicas distribute read queries across multiple database instances, reducing CPU per instance.
A connection pooler can multiplex many application connections into a smaller pool of database connections.

solution.explanation: Each strategy addresses a different facet of the RDS bottleneck. ElastiCache is the most impactful for read-heavy workloads with repeated hot content — serving popular articles directly from an in-memory cache eliminates the database roundtrip entirely, reducing CPU and latency by 80-95% for cacheable content. The cache-aside pattern (check cache → hit or miss → populate on miss) is the most common and flexible implementation. Read Replicas distribute the remaining database read load across multiple instances, which is necessary for queries that cannot be cached (complex joins, large result sets, frequently changing data). RDS Proxy solves the connection exhaustion problem by maintaining a managed connection pool — applications can open and close thousands of short-lived connections while the proxy maintains a smaller pool of long-lived RDS connections, staying well within the database's connection limit. These three strategies are complementary: a large EC2 fleet or Lambda functions benefit from all three simultaneously, with ElastiCache serving the hot cache tier, Read Replicas serving the warm query tier, and RDS Proxy managing the connection efficiency.

methodSignatures.description: Three cache invalidation approaches: (1) TTL expiry — simple, may serve stale data, (2) Write-through — update cache on every write, always fresh but adds write latency, (3) Event-driven invalidation — application deletes/updates cache key when source data changes (most complex but freshest). For article content: TTL is usually sufficient. For account balances: event-driven invalidation or no cache.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: RDS Connection Limits by Instance Type
methodSignatures.description: RDS connection limits scale with instance memory: db.t3.micro ≈ 66 connections, db.t3.medium ≈ 170, db.r5.large ≈ 600, db.r5.4xlarge ≈ 5,000. For Lambda functions creating many concurrent connections, even large RDS instances get overwhelmed. RDS Proxy is essential for Lambda → RDS architectures — it's not optional at scale.

title: ElastiCache Redis vs Memcached: Choosing the Right Engine
description: A development team is deciding between ElastiCache Redis and ElastiCache Memcached for two different use cases: (1) caching user session data that must survive a node failure and support multi-AZ deployment, and (2) a simple object cache for product catalog data that needs to be horizontally scalable with multiple nodes and doesn't need the cached data to survive any node failure. They need to understand the key architectural differences.
hints: Redis supports persistence (RDB snapshots, AOF logs), replication, and Multi-AZ with automatic failover — making it suitable for data that should survive failures.
Memcached is a pure caching solution with no persistence or replication — simpler but loses all data on node failure.
Redis supports advanced data structures (sorted sets, lists, hashes, sets) beyond simple key-value; Memcached supports only string values.

solution.explanation: Redis and Memcached represent two distinct caching philosophies. Redis is a feature-rich in-memory data structure store that happens to be used as a cache — it supports persistence (RDB snapshots and AOF transaction logs), replication, Multi-AZ automatic failover, pub/sub messaging, and rich data structures like sorted sets for real-time leaderboards. These features make Redis appropriate for data that must survive failures and use cases requiring more than simple key-value storage. Memcached is a purpose-built distributed memory cache optimized for the simplest possible caching scenario: multi-threaded for maximum CPU utilization, horizontally scalable by adding nodes, but with absolutely no persistence, replication, or advanced data structures. The choice is clear: if you need durability, replication, failover, or advanced data structures, choose Redis; if you need a simple, maximally efficient pure cache that can afford to lose data on failure, choose Memcached. On the exam, Redis is almost always the answer when any advanced feature is required — Memcached is specifically for the simplest ephemeral caching use cases.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Redis Sorted Sets for Leaderboards
methodSignatures.description: Redis Sorted Sets (ZADD/ZRANGE) store members with an associated score and maintain automatic sort order. This makes real-time leaderboards trivial: ZADD leaderboard 1500 'user123' adds/updates a score; ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 9 returns top 10 players. Operations are O(log N) — extremely efficient even for millions of players. Memcached cannot do this natively.

ElastiCache Redis has two modes: Cluster Mode Disabled (single shard, one primary + up to 5 replicas, max node size limits storage) and Cluster Mode Enabled (multiple shards, each with primary + replicas, horizontally scalable for larger datasets). Use cluster mode for datasets exceeding single-node memory or for read throughput beyond single-shard limits.

title: RDS Backup Strategies: Automated Backups vs Manual Snapshots
description: A financial services company needs to implement a comprehensive backup strategy for their RDS PostgreSQL database. They need to recover from accidental data corruption that may not be discovered until days later, protect against regional disasters, and ensure they can recover to any specific transaction timestamp within the last 7 days. They also need to understand the cost and retention differences between automated backups and manual snapshots.
hints: Automated backups enable point-in-time recovery because RDS continuously backs up transaction logs in addition to daily snapshots.
Manual snapshots persist until you explicitly delete them — unlike automated backups which are automatically deleted after the retention period.
Cross-region backup copies must be explicitly created — they are not created automatically by standard RDS backup settings.

solution.explanation: Automated RDS backups and manual snapshots are complementary — they serve different purposes and have different retention behaviors. Automated backups enable Point-in-Time Recovery by combining daily database snapshots with continuous 5-minute transaction log backups, allowing restoration to any second within the retention window (up to 35 days). However, automated backups are automatically deleted when the RDS instance is deleted or when the retention period expires — they cannot serve long-term compliance retention requirements. Manual snapshots persist indefinitely until explicitly deleted, making them suitable for compliance requirements of 90+ days and for cross-region disaster recovery (snapshots can be copied to any region). A critical operational pitfall is deleting an RDS instance without creating a final snapshot — by default, automated backups are deleted with the instance, meaning you lose your only recovery option. All RDS restoration operations (PITR or snapshot restore) create a NEW RDS instance — there is no in-place restore, which actually makes recovery testing safe since production is unaffected.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: Automated Backup Deletion on Instance Deletion
methodSignatures.description: When you delete an RDS instance without enabling 'final snapshot', ALL automated backups are permanently deleted. Always enable 'Create final snapshot' when deleting production RDS instances. As a safeguard, use IAM policies to prevent deletion without a final snapshot, or use AWS Config rules to alert on this configuration.

methodSignatures.method: Tip: AWS Backup for Cross-Region and Compliance
methodSignatures.description: AWS Backup is a centralized backup service that automates RDS snapshots across regions and accounts, enforces retention policies, and provides compliance reporting.
